title: Nonprofit & Political Law
description: How 501(c)(3)s, 501(c)(4)s, PACs and super PACs differ, and the rules on elections, lobbying, money, disclosure and enforcement that anyone founding, running or funding one should know.
caveat: Prepared October 23, 2026 from statutes, IRS and FEC guidance, court opinions and practitioner guides. US federal law, simplified; states add their own rules. Not legal advice: talk to a nonprofit or election lawyer before acting. AI-written and AI fact-checked; no person has reviewed it.

units.title: The entity menu
units.desc: The main legal structures for advocacy, political and philanthropic money, and what each one can and can't do.

items.p: Match each type of organization to what sets it apart.
pairs: 501(c)(3) charity
Gifts are tax-deductible, but it may never support or oppose a candidate
501(c)(4) social welfare group
Can lobby without limit and do some election work; gifts aren't deductible
Traditional PAC
Gives money directly to candidates, within federal contribution limits
Super PAC
Takes unlimited contributions for independent spending, but can't give to candidates
527 political organization
Tax-code label for groups mainly devoted to influencing who gets elected or appointed, including PACs
items.x: The 501(c) types and 527 are tax-code categories; PACs and super PACs are campaign-finance categories regulated by the FEC, so one group can be both (federal PACs are 527s for tax purposes). People often say '527' to mean a political group that isn't registered with the FEC, such as one working only on state races. Many advocacy groups run a (c)(3), a (c)(4) and a PAC side by side, each with its own money and rules.

items.p: An advocacy group is deciding whether to organize as a 501(c)(3) or a 501(c)(4). What is the core tradeoff between the two?
items.answer: A 501(c)(3) can receive tax-deductible donations (and most foundation money), but it may never support or oppose candidates and can lobby only a limited amount. A 501(c)(4) can lobby without limit on issues tied to its mission and do some election work, but gifts to it aren't tax-deductible.
keys: (c)(3): deductible gifts and most foundation money
(c)(3): no candidate work, limited lobbying
(c)(4): unlimited lobbying and some election work, but gifts aren't deductible
items.x: This is why many groups set up both: the (c)(3) does research, education and limited lobbying with deductible money, and the (c)(4) takes on legislative fights and election work. A private foundation can fund a (c)(4) only for charitable purposes and with extra oversight paperwork ('expenditure responsibility'), so most foundation money goes to (c)(3)s. Gifts to (c)(4)s have been exempt from federal gift tax since 2015.

choice.p: Which best describes the core tradeoff between a 501(c)(3) and a 501(c)(4)?
o: (c)(3): deductible gifts, no candidate work, limited lobbying. (c)(4): unlimited lobbying and some election work, no deductible gifts
(c)(3): may endorse candidates but may not lobby. (c)(4): may lobby freely but may not endorse candidates or run any election ads at all
(c)(3): must publish its donors' names. (c)(4): keeps its donors private but pays income tax on the donations it receives
(c)(3): unlimited lobbying but no foundation grants. (c)(4): may take foundation grants but must register with the FEC first
ow: It's the reverse: a (c)(3) can never endorse, but it can lobby within limits, and a (c)(4) can do some election work.
Public charities and (c)(4)s can keep donor names off their public returns (private foundations can't), and a (c)(4) pays no income tax on donations it receives.
A (c)(3)'s lobbying is limited, and (c)(3)s get most foundation money.

items.p: Five solar-panel installers want to form a tax-exempt group, funded by member dues, to lobby for policies that help their industry. Which type of organization fits best?
o: A 501(c)(6) business league, the form for groups that share a business interest
A 501(c)(4) social welfare group, since it is the type that can lobby without limit
A 501(c)(3) charity, so the companies can deduct their dues as charitable gifts
A 501(c)(5) labor organization, since all its members work in the same trade
ow: A (c)(4) must work for the general welfare of the community; advancing one industry's business interests is what (c)(6) status is for.
A (c)(3) can lobby only a limited amount, and serving its members' businesses would be a private benefit it isn't allowed.
A (c)(5) is an association of workers, such as a union bargaining with employers; these members are companies.
keys: a 501(c)(6) business league (trade association)
for groups with a common business interest
items.x: Trade associations and chambers of commerce are (c)(6)s; unions are (c)(5)s. Like a (c)(4), a (c)(6) may lobby on issues germane to its purpose. If it lobbies or does political work, it may have to tell members what share of their dues paid for it, or else pay a 'proxy tax' (unit 6).

items.p: Super PACs can take unlimited contributions, including from corporations and unions, while traditional PACs face contribution caps. What does a super PAC give up in exchange?
o: It can't give money to candidates or coordinate its spending with them
It can't run ads naming a federal candidate in the 60 days before an election
It must spend at least half its money on nonpartisan voter registration
It can't accept money from individuals, only from corporations, unions and PACs
ow: That blackout once applied to ads paid for by corporations and unions; Citizens United (2010) struck it down, and super PACs run such ads routinely.
There's no required mix of spending; super PACs mostly fund ads and field work for or against candidates.
Individuals can give unlimited amounts too.
keys: can't contribute to candidates
spending must be independent, not coordinated with candidates
items.x: Two 2010 rulings created super PACs: Citizens United v. FEC (the government can't ban independent spending by corporations and unions) and SpeechNow.org v. FEC (individuals' contributions to groups that only spend independently can't be capped; the FEC soon applied this to corporate and union money too). 'Coordinated' means made in cooperation with, or at the request of, a candidate or campaign; a coordinated ad counts as a contribution, subject to limits. For comparison, a multicandidate PAC can give a federal candidate up to $5,000 per election.

items.p: Match each kind of federal PAC to what sets it apart.
pairs: Connected PAC (separate segregated fund)
Set up by a corporation or union, which may pay its overhead and fundraising costs
Traditional nonconnected PAC
No corporate or union sponsor; raises capped contributions and can give to candidates
Hybrid PAC
Keeps a capped account for giving to candidates and an uncapped one for independent spending
Leadership PAC
Controlled by a politician, but separate from that politician's own campaign committee
items.x: Super PACs and hybrid PACs are also nonconnected PACs. A connected PAC may ask for money only from a 'restricted class' of people tied to its sponsor (unit 7). Hybrid PACs date from Carey v. FEC (2011), and the FEC requires their two accounts to be held in separate bank accounts.

items.p: A new group will raise and spend money only to elect candidates to its state legislature, with no federal races. Under federal tax law, what kind of organization is it?
o: A 527 political organization, following state election law rather than FEC rules
A super PAC, which must register with the FEC before it spends money on any race
A 501(c)(4), since state races fall outside the limits on a (c)(4)'s election work
None: federal tax law reaches only groups that are active in federal elections
ow: FEC registration is triggered by raising or spending over $1,000 a year to influence federal elections.
A (c)(4)'s election work can't be its primary activity, and that limit counts state races too.
Section 527 covers groups influencing elections to federal, state and local offices.
keys: a 527 political organization
it follows state campaign-finance law, not FEC rules
items.x: '527' is the tax-code label for any group mainly devoted to influencing who is elected or appointed to office, at any level. A state-level 527 generally files a notice of its status with the IRS (Form 8871) unless it expects under $25,000 a year in receipts or is a state or local candidate or party committee, and some groups that report to a state agency are excused from the IRS's contribution reports.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) in its eighth year gets almost all its money from its founder's yearly gifts, plus a few small donations. Which status will it end up with, and why?
o: Private foundation: one donor's gifts count as public support only up to 2% of the total
Public charity: any 501(c)(3) that runs its own programs, instead of only making grants, is one
Public charity: gifts from individuals all count as public support, whatever their size
Private foundation: every 501(c)(3) becomes one after its first five years
ow: Running programs doesn't settle it; a 501(c)(3) is presumed a private foundation unless it shows broad public support.
Each donor's gifts count only up to 2% of total support, so one big donor can't supply the public share.
Age alone doesn't decide it; after five years a group must pass a public support test, which broadly funded groups do.
keys: private foundation
a single donor's gifts count as public support only up to 2% of total support, so it can't reach one-third public support
items.x: Every 501(c)(3) is presumed to be a private foundation unless it shows it's a public charity. The usual test asks whether at least a third of its support over five years came from the public, government or other public charities (a 10% floor applies if other facts show public character). A new group counts as a public charity for its first five years if it can reasonably expect to pass, and is tested from year six. A second test, for groups that earn fees from their programs, works similarly.

items.p: Name two extra rules a 501(c)(3) faces once it is classified as a private foundation instead of a public charity.
items.answer: Examples: an excise tax on its net investment income; a required yearly payout of about 5% of its investment assets; a ban on most financial dealings with insiders (self-dealing), even at fair prices; excise taxes on its own lobbying and election spending and on some grants (taxable expenditures); limits on business holdings and risky investments.
keys: excise tax on net investment income
required yearly payout of about 5% of investment assets
self-dealing ban on deals with insiders
taxable expenditure rules on lobbying, elections and some grants
limits on business holdings or jeopardizing investments
items.x: These rules are why advocacy groups work to stay public charities. A foundation's own lobbying is a taxable expenditure, so a lobbying-heavy charity reclassified as a foundation would owe excise taxes on its core work. The rules on foundation grants to other groups come in unit 9.

choice.p: Which of these rules applies to a private foundation but not to a public charity?
o: It must pay out about 5% of its investment assets each year for charitable purposes
It must file something with the IRS every year, even if its income is very small
It may never support or oppose a candidate for public office in any election, at any level
Its directors owe the organization duties of care and loyalty under state nonprofit law
ow: Both must file yearly: small public charities file the Form 990-N e-Postcard, and foundations file Form 990-PF whatever their size.
The ban on campaign intervention applies to every 501(c)(3).
Fiduciary duties come from state law and apply to every nonprofit board.

items.p: In 2015 Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan pledged about $45 billion in Facebook shares to a new philanthropy set up as an LLC instead of a private foundation. What did they give up by choosing an LLC?
o: The tax deduction a foundation would have given them when they moved the shares in
The right to fund political campaigns and lobbying, which an LLC is barred from doing
Control of the money, which under LLC law passes to an independent board of managers
Privacy, since an LLC must publish every grant it makes on a public IRS return
ow: An LLC can fund politics and lobbying; it's a private foundation that faces tax penalties for those.
An LLC stays under its owners' control; the couple kept control of how the money is used.
An LLC files no public Form 990-PF; a private foundation does, listing its grants.
keys: the upfront charitable tax deduction
no tax benefit when the shares moved into the LLC; deductions come only when it gives to charity
items.x: Zuckerberg wrote that they 'receive no tax benefit from transferring our shares' and that they would owe capital gains tax when the LLC sold shares. In return, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative could fund nonprofits, make private investments and take part in policy debates without private-foundation rules. The owners get a deduction only when the LLC itself gives to a charity.

items.p: A donor wants one vehicle that can make charitable grants, fund a 501(c)(4)'s lobbying campaign and invest in a mission-driven startup. Why might her adviser suggest an LLC over a private foundation?
o: It can do all three without the foundation rules on lobbying, insider deals and payouts
Gifts into an LLC are deductible at once, at higher limits than gifts to a foundation
An LLC pays no capital gains tax when it sells the stock that its owner put into it
An LLC's grants to a 501(c)(4) become tax-deductible, unlike a foundation's grants
ow: Putting money into an LLC earns no deduction; the donor deducts only when the LLC gives to a charity.
The LLC's gains are taxed to its owners; Zuckerberg said they would pay capital gains tax when the LLC sold their shares.
Money given to a (c)(4) isn't a charitable deduction, whatever vehicle it comes from.
keys: an LLC isn't bound by private-foundation rules
it can fund lobbying, (c)(4)s, politics and for-profit investments, with no payout requirement
items.x: The price is the upfront deduction. An LLC also files no public Form 990-PF, so its grants and investments stay private unless its owners disclose them. A private foundation, by contrast, owes excise taxes on its own lobbying and election spending and must pay out about 5% of its investment assets a year.

units.title: Starting up
units.desc: Forming the organization, winning IRS recognition, registering with states, and raising money under a fiscal sponsor before you have your own exemption.

items.p: Put the usual steps for starting a new 501(c)(3) charity in order.
items: File articles of incorporation with the state
Get an employer identification number (EIN) from the IRS
Apply for recognition of exemption on Form 1023
Receive the IRS determination letter recognizing 501(c)(3) status
items.x: The IRS says not to get an EIN until the organization legally exists: applying for one tells the IRS you're formed and starts the three-year clock for automatic revocation (unit 3). Form 1023 is filed online through Pay.gov; as of October 2026 the fee is $600, or $275 for the short Form 1023-EZ.

items.p: Very small charities can apply on the short Form 1023-EZ by attesting that their articles of incorporation meet IRS rules, without sending the articles in. A 2019 study by the National Taxpayer Advocate checked a sample of approved groups' articles. What did it find?
o: Close to half had articles that didn't meet the legal test for a 501(c)(3)
Very few failed, since applicants must attest that their articles comply
About one in ten failed, and almost all fixed their articles within a year
None failed, since the IRS reviews every short-form filer before approving it
ow: Attestation didn't prevent it: 159 of 347 approved groups in the 20-state sample had articles that failed the test.
The rate was much higher, about 46%; earlier studies of the same states found 26% to 42%.
The IRS reviews only a random sample before approval; the rest are approved on the applicant's attestation.
keys: close to half (about 46%)
their articles didn't meet the organizational test
items.x: The organizational test requires a 501(c)(3)'s founding document to limit its purposes to exempt ones and to dedicate its assets to exempt purposes, including if it dissolves. The Taxpayer Advocate called these approvals erroneous, since such groups don't qualify. So an approval letter doesn't confirm a group's articles are valid; founders should check them against the organizational test (next card).

items.p: A founder's draft articles of incorporation say the new nonprofit may 'engage in any lawful activity.' Why will a nonprofit lawyer insist on changing this before the group applies for 501(c)(3) status?
o: The articles must limit its purposes to exempt ones, and this wording is broader
The IRS requires articles to list each program the group plans to run in its first years
Without express permission in the articles, a 501(c)(3) may not do any lobbying at all
States tax any corporation whose articles use that phrase as a for-profit business
ow: Articles state purposes; the exemption application describes planned activities separately.
No permission clause is needed to lobby a little, and articles expressly authorizing substantial lobbying would fail the test.
The problem is federal: the IRS reads the stated purposes to decide whether the group is organized exclusively for exempt ones.
keys: articles must limit purposes to 501(c)(3) exempt purposes
'any lawful activity' is broader, so it fails the organizational test
items.x: Under the organizational test, articles must limit purposes to exempt ones, must not expressly empower more than an insubstantial amount of other activity, and must dedicate assets to exempt purposes. IRS instructions give model clauses, including one sending assets on dissolution to other exempt purposes or to a government for a public purpose.

items.p: A new tenant-organizing charity expects about $40,000 a year in gifts for its first three years and owns little beyond a laptop. Which application can it use?
o: Form 1023-EZ, since it projects $50,000 or less a year and has $250,000 or less in assets
Only the full Form 1023, because groups that organize or advocate can't use the short form
Form 1023-EZ, since any group under $250,000 in yearly revenue may use it
Form 8976, the short notice small groups file instead of applying for 501(c)(3) status
ow: The eligibility worksheet rules out types such as LLCs, supporting organizations and would-be churches, schools and hospitals, but advocacy isn't one of them.
$250,000 is the asset limit; projected gross receipts must stay at or under $50,000 in each of the next three years.
Form 8976 is the notice for new 501(c)(4)s; a charity applies on Form 1023 or 1023-EZ.
keys: Form 1023-EZ
projected gross receipts of $50,000 or less a year and assets of $250,000 or less
items.x: The EZ worksheet also asks about past receipts and lists about 30 other disqualifiers. As of October 2026 the fee is $275, against $600 for the full Form 1023. Groups (other than private foundations) whose gross receipts are normally $5,000 or less don't have to apply at all to be treated as 501(c)(3)s.

items.p: A new nonprofit formed in January 2026 has been taking donations while it prepares its 501(c)(3) application. If the IRS approves it, what decides whether those early gifts were tax-deductible?
o: Whether it filed Form 1023 within 27 months of forming, making approval retroactive
Nothing: only gifts received after the IRS approval letter arrives can ever be deducted
Whether each donor attached a pending-status statement to their own tax return
Whether it registered with its state's charity regulator before taking any gifts
ow: Approval of a timely application reaches back to the date the group was formed, so earlier gifts count.
There's no such donor form; deductibility depends on the group's status.
State registration rules govern asking for money in that state; they don't decide whether a gift is federally deductible.
keys: file Form 1023 within 27 months of formation
recognition is then retroactive to the formation date
items.x: If Form 1023 is filed within 27 months of the end of the month the group was formed, the IRS generally treats its exemption as starting on the formation date. File later and it usually starts on the filing date, unless the IRS grants relief for good cause. Groups that want to raise money before applying often use a fiscal sponsor: an existing 501(c)(3) that receives gifts for the project and pays for its work.

items.p: A newly formed 501(c)(4) asks whether it needs IRS approval before it starts operating. What does federal law require?
o: A notice on Form 8976 within 60 days; an IRS determination letter is optional
A full application on Form 1023 within 27 months of forming, the same as for a charity
Nothing at all: 501(c)(4)s are exempt automatically and never need to contact the IRS
Registration with the FEC before it accepts membership dues or gifts of any size
ow: Form 1023 is the charity application; a (c)(4) may apply on Form 1024-A but isn't required to.
Section 506 requires every new (c)(4) to notify the IRS within 60 days; a late notice costs $20 a day, up to $5,000.
FEC registration depends on federal election spending, not on being a (c)(4).
keys: file a Form 8976 notice within 60 days of forming
applying for a determination letter (Form 1024-A) is optional
items.x: The notice costs $50 and only puts the group on record; it isn't a ruling on exempt status. Filing Form 1024-A doesn't replace it. Unlike its exemption application and annual returns, a (c)(4)'s Form 8976 notice doesn't have to be shown to the public.

items.p: Match each IRS filing to what it does.
pairs: Form 1023
Full application for recognition as a 501(c)(3) charity
Form 1023-EZ
Short 501(c)(3) application for groups with very small budgets
Form 8976
Required notice that a new group is operating as a 501(c)(4)
Form 1024-A
Optional application for an IRS letter confirming 501(c)(4) status
Form 8871
Notice that a political group is claiming 527 status
items.x: The asymmetry matters: a would-be charity generally must apply to be treated as a 501(c)(3) (churches and groups with gross receipts normally $5,000 or less are excepted), while a (c)(4) can operate after filing a notice. A 527 skips Form 8871 if it reports to the FEC as a political committee, expects under $25,000 a year in receipts, or is a state or local candidate or party committee.

items.p: A new 501(c)(3) based in Ohio plans a mail and email fundraising appeal to supporters in California, New York and a dozen other states. Beyond its IRS status, what must it check first?
o: Whether each state requires charities to register before soliciting its residents
Nothing more: IRS recognition covers a charity's fundraising in every state
Only Ohio's rules, since states can regulate only charities formed under their own laws
Whether it has registered with the FEC, which oversees appeals sent across state lines
ow: Charity fundraising is regulated by the states, and most require charities soliciting their residents to register and report each year.
Registration follows where you solicit: California, for example, requires out-of-state charities doing business there to register.
The FEC regulates federal election money; charity fundraising is a state matter.
keys: state charitable solicitation registration
most states require registering before soliciting their residents, wherever the charity is based
items.x: As of 2026, practitioner counts run from 36 states plus DC to about 40 jurisdictions, depending on how exemptions are counted. California requires registration with the attorney general's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers within 30 days of first receiving charitable assets. Whether a website's donate button alone triggers registration varies by state. Under the Charleston Principles, nonbinding 2001 guidance from state charity officials, a button alone usually doesn't, but directing residents to it does.

items.p: Organizers want to raise tax-deductible money next month for a short voter-education project and don't plan to create an organization of their own. What's the usual way to do this?
o: Find a fiscal sponsor: a 501(c)(3) that takes gifts for the project and keeps control of them
Collect gifts in an organizer's account now; donors can deduct them once the IRS approves the project
Form an LLC first, since gifts to an LLC run by volunteers are deductible while it waits for approval
Ask donors to give through a 501(c)(4) partner, whose gifts are deductible for education projects
ow: A gift to an individual isn't deductible; only gifts to a qualifying organization are.
Money put into an LLC isn't a charitable gift; a deduction comes only when money reaches a charity.
Gifts to a 501(c)(4) aren't deductible, whatever the project.
keys: a fiscal sponsor
an existing 501(c)(3) receives the gifts for the project and keeps ultimate control over them
items.x: The sponsor usually keeps an administrative fee and takes legal responsibility for how the money is used, so it vets projects. Because the money is the sponsor's, a 501(c)(3) sponsor can't let a project do what it couldn't do itself, such as endorse candidates. If the organizers later form their own group, applying within 27 months makes its exemption retroactive (previous lesson).

items.p: In fiscal sponsorship, what's the main difference between a 'Model A' and a 'Model C' arrangement?
o: In A the project is part of the sponsor, which employs its staff; in C it's a separate grantee
In A the sponsor takes no fee at all; in C it keeps a set percentage of every gift the project brings in
In A donors decide how their gifts are spent; in C the sponsor's board makes every spending decision
A is for projects that will become charities, and C is for projects that will become 501(c)(4) groups
ow: Sponsors in both models usually keep an administrative fee; the difference is who legally owns and runs the project.
In both models the sponsor must keep ultimate discretion over the money; donors can't direct it.
The letters describe the legal structure, not the project's future tax status.
keys: Model A: the project is a program of the sponsor, with no separate legal existence
Model C: a separate entity that receives pre-approved grants from the sponsor
items.x: The letters come from attorney Gregory Colvin's guide to fiscal sponsorship. In Model A the sponsor holds the project's assets, liabilities, staff and volunteers, so the project's actions, including any lobbying, are legally the sponsor's; Colvin called it the model 'least exposed to IRS challenge.' In Model C the project runs as its own entity, handles its own liability, and receives regranted money.

items.p: Why must a fiscal sponsor keep real control over the money it raises for a project, instead of passing every gift straight through as the project directs?
items.answer: If the sponsor is a mere conduit, the IRS can disregard it and treat each gift as made directly to the project, which isn't a 501(c)(3). Donors then lose their charitable deduction.
keys: a mere conduit: the IRS treats the gift as going straight to the project
donors lose the charitable deduction
items.x: Practitioners say the sponsor must have 'ultimate discretion and control' over whether to spend gifts itself or regrant them. Sponsorship agreements typically let the sponsor withhold grants if a project breaches its terms or seems likely to divert funds. For a private foundation funding the project through a sponsor, a conduit finding can also trigger its oversight duties for grants to non-charities.

choice.p: Why must a fiscal sponsor keep real control over money raised for a project?
o: Otherwise it's a mere conduit, and donors can lose their charitable deduction
Otherwise the project must register with the IRS as a 527 political organization
Otherwise the sponsor owes unrelated business income tax on the gifts it passes on
Otherwise the IRS counts the gifts toward the sponsor's lobbying limit
ow: 527 status turns on election activity, not on how a sponsor handles gifts.
Donations aren't business income; that tax applies to regularly run businesses unrelated to the mission.
Lobbying limits depend on spending to influence legislation, not on who directs the money.

units.title: Governance and staying exempt
units.desc: What board members owe, the rules on deals with insiders and executive pay, which annual return to file, and the slips that cost groups their exemption.

items.p: Match each fiduciary duty of a nonprofit board member to an example of meeting it.
pairs: Duty of care
Reading the audit and asking questions before voting to accept it
Duty of loyalty
Disclosing a family tie to a vendor and sitting out the vote on its contract
Duty of obedience
Blocking a new program that falls outside the purposes in the group's articles
items.x: These duties come from state law, and state attorneys general can go to court to enforce them (unit 10). Minnesota's attorney general, for example, describes loyalty as 'an absolute duty of complete, undivided loyalty' and care as the care 'an ordinarily prudent person' would use. Directors can hand daily work to staff but remain responsible for overseeing it.

items.p: A board member's printing company bids for her nonprofit's printing contract, and she tells the board. What should happen next under standard conflict-of-interest practice?
o: She sits out the discussion and vote; the rest approve only if the deal is fair
The board rejects the bid, since a nonprofit may never contract with its own board members
She may vote after disclosing her interest, since disclosure alone resolves the conflict
The contract can go ahead without a board vote if her price beats the other bids
ow: A public charity may make such a deal if it's fair, disclosed and approved by members without a conflict; private foundations face a far stricter ban.
Disclosure is the first step; she should also stay out of the deliberation and the vote.
A low price helps show fairness, but members without a conflict should still approve the deal and record why.
keys: she recuses from the discussion and vote
members without a conflict approve it only if it's fair and reasonable to the nonprofit
items.x: Minnesota's attorney general, for example, says such a deal may be permissible if it was fair and reasonable, fully disclosed, and approved in good faith by directors without a conflict. In a private foundation, by contrast, buying goods or services from a board member or her company is generally banned as 'self-dealing,' even at a fair price.

items.p: Does federal tax law require a 501(c)(3) to adopt a written conflict-of-interest policy?
o: No, but Form 990 asks whether it has one, and the IRS says such policies help compliance
Yes: the IRS automatically revokes the exemption of any group that has no written policy
Yes, but only for groups big enough that they must file the full Form 990 each year
No, and Form 990 asks nothing about how a group is governed or what policies it has
ow: No federal rule requires the policy; automatic revocation is for missing three annual returns in a row.
Even full-990 filers aren't required to have one; they must only say whether they do.
Part VI of Form 990 asks about the board, policies and practices, and the answers are public.
keys: no federal requirement
Form 990 asks whether the group has one, and the IRS considers such policies to improve compliance
items.x: The 990 instructions say these policies generally aren't required under the tax code, but the IRS 'considers such policies and procedures to generally improve tax compliance.' Some states go further: New York's nonprofit law requires boards to adopt one.

items.p: A board is about to set its new executive director's salary at $180,000. One member asks whether the figure will become public. What's the answer?
o: Yes: Form 990 lists the pay of officers and key employees, and anyone may ask for a copy
No: pay goes on a confidential schedule, the same way donor names do
Only if the group is a private foundation, since public charities' returns are confidential
Only if the salary is above the federal cap on nonprofit executive pay
ow: Donor names can be withheld from the public copy; pay reported on the 990 can't.
Public charities' returns are public too, for three years from their due dates.
There's no federal cap on nonprofit pay; the test is whether pay is reasonable (next lesson).
keys: yes, it will be public
Form 990 reports pay of officers, directors and key employees, and the return must be shared on request
items.x: Form 990 lists every current officer, director and trustee whatever their pay, key employees paid over $150,000, and the five highest-paid other employees over $100,000. A group must give copies of its last three years' returns and its exemption application to anyone who asks.

items.p: In 1989 the Tax Court reviewed a school that trained people to work on political campaigns. It grew out of a training course run by one party's House campaign committee, and its graduates who took campaign jobs mostly worked for that party's candidates. Did it qualify as a 501(c)(3)?
o: No: it gave more than incidental benefit to one party and its candidates
Yes: teaching campaign skills is educational, and no insider was overpaid
No: training campaign staff counts as intervening in a political campaign
Yes: a charity's party ties matter only if it endorses candidates itself
ow: Educational work still fails if it serves private interests more than incidentally, even with no insider profit.
The court rested its ruling on private benefit, a rule separate from the campaign ban.
Under the private benefit rule, serving a party can disqualify a group even without endorsements.
keys: no, it did not qualify
it gave more than incidental private benefit to one party's candidates and committees
items.x: In American Campaign Academy v. Commissioner, the school grew out of a National Republican Congressional Committee course, and one of its three initial directors was the NRCC's executive director. It never showed that graduates worked for Democrats, so the court inferred they served Republicans and held that its benefit to Republican candidates and entities was more than incidental. The private benefit rule applies the same way to a group serving any party.

items.p: What separates the ban on private inurement from the ban on private benefit for a 501(c)(3)?
items.answer: Private inurement means insiders, such as founders, directors and top staff, getting the charity's earnings or assets beyond fair value, and any amount can cost exemption. Private benefit reaches anyone, including outsiders, but only benefit that is more than incidental to the public purpose is barred.
keys: inurement: insiders, and any amount is forbidden
private benefit: anyone, including outsiders; incidental benefit is allowed
items.x: CRS notes the IRS has said 'any amount of inurement is grounds for revocation,' while it treats incidental private benefit as permissible. A charity can pay staff and buy from vendors at fair prices; trouble starts with overpaying insiders or serving private interests more than incidentally. The excise taxes in the next card are the IRS's tool short of revocation.

choice.p: Which best describes the difference between private inurement and private benefit?
o: Inurement: insiders, with no minimum; private benefit: anyone, but incidental benefit is allowed
Inurement is a crime the Justice Department prosecutes; private benefit is only a civil tax matter
Inurement applies only to private foundations; private benefit applies only to public charities
Inurement covers cash payments; private benefit covers only gifts of property, services or facilities
ow: Both are tax rules; the IRS enforces them through revocation and, for deals with insiders, excise taxes.
Both rules apply to every 501(c)(3), public charity or foundation.
Either can involve cash or other benefits; the line is who benefits and how much.

items.p: A public charity's board knowingly approves paying its founder twice what similar groups pay for the same job, and the IRS finds the pay excessive. Under the 'intermediate sanctions' rules, who owes tax?
o: The founder owes 25% of the excess; board members who approved may owe 10%
The charity owes a penalty equal to the excess, paid from its general funds
No one; the IRS's only remedy is to revoke the charity's tax-exempt status
The donors whose gifts paid the salary owe tax on the deductions they took
ow: The charity itself doesn't pay this tax; it falls on the insider and the managers who approved the deal.
These excise taxes were created as an alternative to revocation, though the IRS can still revoke in serious cases.
Donors aren't penalized for a charity's pay decisions.
keys: the founder (a disqualified person) pays 25% of the excess benefit, rising to 200% if not repaid
managers who knowingly approved owe 10%, capped at $20,000 per transaction
items.x: Section 4958 covers public charities and 501(c)(4)s; private foundations have the stricter self-dealing rules instead. If the founder doesn't repay the excess in time, a second tax of 200% applies. 'Intermediate' means short of revocation, which remains possible.

items.p: A charity's board is setting its executive director's pay. Which process gives it the strongest protection if the IRS later argues the pay was excessive?
o: Members with no conflict approve it in advance using comparable pay data, and record why
The full board, including the director, approves it after an outside auditor reviews the books
The board keeps the pay below the federal salary cap that applies to nonprofit executives
The board approves it at year end, once it sees how much money the director helped raise
ow: The director has a conflict and shouldn't vote, and a financial audit says nothing about whether pay is reasonable.
There's no federal cap on nonprofit pay; the question is whether pay is reasonable for the job.
Approval must come before the pay is set, based on comparable pay data rather than results after the fact.
keys: approved in advance by board members without a conflict
relying on comparability data
documented at the time
items.x: These three steps create a 'rebuttable presumption' that pay is reasonable: the IRS can then impose excise taxes only if it develops enough evidence to rebut the comparability data. Groups with under $1 million in annual gross receipts can rely on pay data from three comparable organizations.

items.p: Match each annual IRS return to the organizations that file it.
pairs: Form 990-N (e-Postcard)
Groups with gross receipts normally $50,000 or less
Form 990-EZ
Gross receipts under $200,000 and total assets under $500,000
Form 990
Gross receipts of $200,000 or more, or assets of $500,000 or more
Form 990-PF
Every private foundation, whatever its size
Form 990-T
Exempt groups with $1,000 or more in gross unrelated business income
items.x: Churches are excused from the annual return; almost everyone else files something each year, however small. Form 990-T is filed on top of the regular return, and a 501(c)(3)'s 990-T is public too.

items.p: A small 501(c)(3), recognized in 2020 and taking in about $20,000 a year, has filed nothing with the IRS since, believing groups that small are excused. What has happened to its status?
o: It lost its exemption automatically after three missed years and must apply again
Nothing: groups with receipts under $50,000 don't have to file anything with the IRS
It owes daily late-filing penalties, but its exemption continues until the IRS audits it
Its state attorney general can revoke its federal exemption at the next annual renewal
ow: Groups that small must still file the short electronic Form 990-N each year.
Missing three years in a row ends exemption automatically, with no audit or hearing first.
Only the IRS controls federal exemption; states oversee charity registration and charitable assets.
keys: exemption automatically revoked after three consecutive years of not filing
it must apply to be reinstated
items.x: Revocation takes effect on the original due date of the third missed return, and the group's name goes on a public IRS list; once it's listed, new gifts aren't deductible. A 2019 amendment requires the IRS to warn a group after two missed years. The clock can start before a group even applies: the IRS treats an EIN application as a sign the group has been formed.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) think tank has four sources of income. Which one is most likely to be taxed as unrelated business income?
o: A year-round catering business, run by paid staff, that serves corporate events
Interest and dividends on the reserve fund it keeps in a brokerage account
A thrift shop, staffed by paid employees, that sells clothing donated by its supporters
Rent from leasing two floors of an office building it owns outright, with no mortgage
ow: Dividends, interest and similar investment income are excluded from the tax.
Selling merchandise that was substantially all donated is excluded, even with paid staff.
Rent from real property is generally excluded, unless the property is debt-financed.
keys: the catering business
a regularly run business unrelated to the mission, and no exclusion applies
items.x: The tax code excludes most passive income (dividends, interest, royalties, rent from real estate) and some activities, such as businesses run substantially by volunteers and sales of donated goods. Royalties for licensing a group's name or logo are usually excluded too. Taxable income is taxed at corporate rates.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) think tank starts selling IT support to local businesses year-round, using paid staff, and spends every dollar of profit on its research. Why is that profit still taxable?
items.answer: Whether a business is 'related' depends on whether the activity itself advances the exempt purpose, not on how its profits are used. IT support doesn't advance the research mission, so profit from this regularly run business is unrelated business income.
keys: relatedness depends on the activity itself, not on how profits are spent
a regularly run business unrelated to the mission produces taxable unrelated business income
items.x: The tax code says relatedness is judged 'aside from' the group's need for income 'or the use it makes of the profits.' Income is unrelated if it comes from a trade or business, regularly carried on, that isn't substantially related to the mission. The IRS's example of an occasional activity: a hospital auxiliary's sandwich stand at a two-week state fair isn't 'regularly' carried on.

choice.p: Why is a think tank's profit from selling IT support taxable, even though it all funds research?
o: Whether a business is related depends on the activity itself, not on how its profits are spent
All business income of a 501(c)(3) is taxable, whether or not the activity relates to its mission
The profit is taxable only because the think tank didn't register the business with its state
The profit counts as private inurement, since staff are paid to do the work
ow: Income from a business that itself advances the exempt purpose isn't taxed, even if it earns a profit.
State registration has nothing to do with it; this is the federal unrelated business income tax.
Paying reasonable wages isn't inurement; the issue is that the business is unrelated to the mission.

units.title: (c)(3)s and elections
units.desc: Why a charity can never back or oppose a candidate, and how it can still register voters, host forums, publish guides and speak on issues during campaigns.

items.p: Four days before the 1992 election, a church ran full-page newspaper ads urging Christians not to vote for Bill Clinton. The IRS revoked its tax exemption, and the church sued, citing religious freedom. What did the federal appeals court decide in 2000?
o: It upheld the revocation, noting the church could set up a separate (c)(4) and PAC for political work
It restored the exemption, holding that a church's political ads are protected religious exercise
It restored the exemption because the ads ran in newspapers, outside the church's worship services
It sent the case back, ruling that the IRS must try a smaller excise tax before revoking an exemption
ow: The court found no substantial burden on religious exercise, because the church could still speak politically through a separate (c)(4) and its PAC.
Urging readers not to vote for a named candidate is campaign intervention wherever it appears.
No such sequence is required. The excise tax and revocation are separate tools, and the court upheld the revocation.
keys: the court upheld the revocation
the church could form a separate (c)(4), with a PAC, for political work
items.x: Branch Ministries v. Rossotti (D.C. Cir. 2000). Because the church could create a related (c)(4), whose gifts aren't deductible, and that group could form a PAC, the court found the church's religious exercise wasn't substantially burdened. The court relied on a 1983 Supreme Court case on charity lobbying (unit 5). The ban applies the same way to charities and churches on every side of politics.

items.p: What kind of election-season activity may a 501(c)(3) do?
o: Run a voter registration drive open to everyone that favors no party or candidate
Endorse a candidate in its newsletter, as long as it spends no extra money doing it
Give money to a super PAC that runs ads for candidates who back its cause
Publish ratings of the candidates on its issues, timed to come out before the vote
ow: The ban covers any statement for or against a candidate, whether or not it costs money.
Funding a political committee is campaign intervention, which is barred outright.
Rating candidates favors some over others, so the IRS treats it as campaign intervention.
keys: nonpartisan voter work that favors no candidate or party, such as voter registration open to everyone
items.x: Section 501(c)(3) bars groups that 'participate in, or intervene in' any campaign for or against a candidate, and the IRS calls the ban absolute; breaking it can cost the group its exemption and bring excise taxes. Nonpartisan voter registration, get-out-the-vote drives, candidate forums and unbiased voter guides are allowed. In 2025 the IRS asked a court to approve a deal letting two churches endorse candidates during worship, but a federal judge dismissed the case in March 2026 without approving it. The plaintiffs appealed; as of October 2026 the ban still applies.

items.p: A charity's board approves paying for mailers that attack a city council candidate. Besides putting the charity's exemption at risk, what penalty does the tax code add?
o: An excise tax on the spending, owed by the charity, plus a smaller one on managers who knowingly approved it
A fine from the Federal Election Commission, which polices campaign spending by charities in races at every level
A clawback of donors' past deductions, which the IRS collects from each donor in proportion to their gifts
Nothing more: revoking exemption is the only sanction the IRS has against a charity's campaign spending
ow: The FEC enforces federal campaign finance law and doesn't oversee city races. This penalty comes from section 4955 of the tax code.
Section 4955's tax falls on the charity and on managers who agreed to the spending; donors aren't taxed under it.
Section 4955 adds an excise tax, so the IRS can penalize the spending without revoking exemption, or on top of revoking it.
keys: an excise tax on the political spending, owed by the charity
a smaller excise tax on managers who knowingly agreed to it
items.x: Section 4955 taxes each political expenditure at 10%, rising to 100% if it isn't corrected in time. A manager who knowingly agreed owes 2.5% (capped at $5,000 per expenditure), rising to 50% (capped at $10,000) for refusing to agree to correct it. The ban covers candidates for any public office, local races included. Unit 10 covers how the IRS examines and revokes exemption.

items.p: A charity wants to urge voters to approve a state ballot initiative raising the minimum wage. How does the campaign ban apply?
o: It doesn't: the ban covers candidates, so this is lobbying, allowed within the charity's lobbying limit
It applies fully, because telling voters how to vote in any election is campaign intervention
It applies unless the charity gives equal space to arguments for and against the initiative
It doesn't, and the work is unlimited, since ballot measures count as neither campaigns nor legislation
ow: The ban covers campaigns for or against candidates for public office, and a ballot measure has no candidate.
Balanced material counts as voter education, which is unlimited. A charity may also take a side, and that counts as lobbying.
The IRS treats ballot measures as legislation, with voters acting as the legislature, so advocacy counts toward the lobbying limit.
keys: the campaign ban covers only candidates, so it doesn't apply
advocacy on a ballot measure counts as lobbying, within the charity's lobbying limit
items.x: The IRS defines legislation to include a 'referendum, ballot initiative, constitutional amendment, or similar procedure.' Under the 501(h) rules (unit 5), urging voters to back or reject a measure is direct lobbying, because the voters are the legislature. States may also require disclosure reports from groups that spend on ballot measures.

items.p: Shortly before an election, an environmental charity phones voters in a state legislative district. Callers ask each voter's view on the race's main environmental issue and offer rides to the polls only to those who side with the challenger. Is this allowed?
o: No: steering get-out-the-vote help to one candidate's likely voters favors that candidate
Yes: get-out-the-vote drives are allowed, and no caller told anyone whom to vote for
Yes, as long as the calls were paid for with unrestricted money and no grant funds
No: a charity may register voters but may never run a get-out-the-vote drive of any kind
ow: Get-out-the-vote work is allowed only when nonpartisan. Choosing whom to help by how they lean favors one side without naming it.
The funding source doesn't change what the activity does; the ban covers any money the charity spends.
The IRS allows nonpartisan get-out-the-vote drives. The problem here is the targeting.
keys: not allowed: it's campaign intervention
the help was aimed at one candidate's supporters
items.x: This is Situation 2 in Revenue Ruling 2007-41, the IRS's main guide to the ban. In its Situation 1, a voter registration booth at a state fair that mentioned no candidate or party was fine. The test is whether the activity, through its content or its targeting, favors a candidate.

items.p: Weeks before an election, a land-conservation charity mails voters across the state a guide showing how each incumbent voted on five conservation bills it cares about. It endorses no one. What is the risk?
o: A guide on the group's own issues, mailed widely during a campaign, can count as backing candidates
None: lawmakers' voting records are public facts, so publishing them can never be campaign intervention
Only that it must mail the guide to every registered voter, so that no group of voters is favored
None, as long as the guide carries a statement that the charity endorses no candidate for office
ow: The IRS weighs which issues are covered, the timing and the distribution; selected votes released mid-campaign can favor candidates.
Wider distribution during a campaign makes it worse: the IRS treated broad mailing to the electorate as a sign of electioneering.
In the IRS's own example, a guide with no endorsement at all still counted as intervention. What matters is issues, timing and audience.
keys: a narrow set of the group's issues, distributed widely during a campaign, can be campaign intervention
even with no endorsement
items.x: Revenue Ruling 78-248 contrasted a compilation of every member's votes 'on major legislation involving a wide range of subjects,' which was fine, with one on 'selected land conservation issues' mailed widely during a campaign, which was intervention. A charity can publish its scorecard after the session ends, in its regular newsletter to its usual readers, if it isn't geared to an election (Revenue Ruling 80-282). Rating candidates is barred outright.

items.p: A charity plans a candidate forum before a state senate election. Name two features that help keep it nonpartisan.
items.answer: Any two of: invite every legally qualified candidate; have an independent, nonpartisan panel prepare the questions; cover a broad range of issues; give each candidate an equal chance to speak; keep the moderator from implying approval or disapproval of any candidate.
keys: invite every legally qualified candidate
an independent, nonpartisan panel prepares the questions
a broad range of issues
each candidate gets an equal opportunity to speak
a neutral moderator
items.x: These factors come from Revenue Ruling 86-95, which says no single one decides the case. Where inviting every candidate is impractical, the IRS has accepted reasonable, objective criteria applied to all, such as a polling threshold. Inviting candidates one at a time also works if each gets the same format (Revenue Ruling 2007-41, Situation 7). No campaign fundraising should happen at the event.

choice.p: Which of these helps keep a charity's candidate forum nonpartisan?
o: Inviting every legally qualified candidate and giving each the same time to answer
Asking each candidate to say whether they back the charity's own platform
Having the charity's director press candidates with follow-ups on the charity's issue
Limiting the questions to the charity's own issue, so the forum stays on its mission
ow: The IRS lists asking candidates to agree or disagree with the group's positions as a sign of bias.
Questions should come from an independent panel, and a moderator who signals approval or disapproval weighs against the forum.
The IRS's model forum covered a broad range of issues. A narrow agenda can suggest bias, as with a narrow voter guide.

items.p: A hospital charity invites its congressman, who is running for reelection, to speak at the opening of a new wing. What would most likely turn the event into campaign intervention?
o: He talks about his reelection campaign and asks the audience for their votes
He is introduced by his official title and talks about the federal grant that helped build the wing
The opening falls in the final months before the election
The hospital doesn't also invite the congressman's opponent
ow: Appearing in his official role and discussing the project, with no mention of the race, is what the IRS's example allowed.
In the IRS's example the event fell during the campaign and was still fine, because nothing tied it to the race.
Equal invitations are needed when someone appears as a candidate. An official appearing in his official role needn't be matched.
keys: mentioning his campaign or the election, asking for votes, or campaign fundraising at the event
items.x: Revenue Ruling 2007-41, Situation 11: a congressman seeking reelection attended a hospital groundbreaking, neither he nor the hospital mentioned the campaign, and no fundraising occurred, so there was no intervention. When someone appears as a candidate, the charity should give rivals an equal opportunity (Situations 7 and 9).

items.p: Six weeks before a governor's reelection, an education charity runs radio ads attacking his school-funding record, an issue his challenger is campaigning on. No vote on school funding is scheduled, and the ads never mention the election. How would the IRS likely see this?
o: As campaign intervention: it names a candidate near the election on an issue dividing the race
As lawful issue advocacy, since the ads never mention voting, the election or the challenger
As lobbying, since school funding is set by the legislature, so it counts only toward lobbying limits
As lawful, since a charity may criticize any sitting official's record as long as it is accurate
ow: An express call to vote isn't required. Naming a candidate close to the election on an issue that sets the candidates apart can be enough.
An ad can be lobbying and campaign intervention at once. With no bill or vote pending, the IRS treated a similar ad as intervention.
Charities may criticize officials' policies, but timing and context can turn criticism of a candidate into intervention.
keys: likely campaign intervention
names a candidate, close to the election, on an issue dividing the candidates, with no legislative event or ongoing series
items.x: This tracks Revenue Ruling 2007-41, Situation 15. In Situation 14, by contrast, a university's ad urging a senator to vote for a bill was fine: it was timed to a scheduled Senate vote and didn't mention the election. A (c)(4) faces similar factors when deciding whether an ad counts as political spending (unit 6).

items.p: A charity wants to keep running ads that name an incumbent senator on its issue during her reelection campaign. Name two features that make such ads less likely to count as campaign intervention.
items.answer: Any two of: tie each ad to a legislative event, such as a scheduled vote on a named bill; make the ads part of an ongoing series that began before the campaign; leave out any mention of voting or the election; stick to issues that aren't dividing lines between the candidates.
keys: timed to a legislative event such as a scheduled vote
part of an ongoing series
no mention of voting or the election
the issue isn't one that distinguishes the candidates
items.x: Revenue Ruling 2007-41 lists these factors and says all the facts and circumstances must be weighed. In 2025 a federal court called a similar multi-factor test too vague as applied to one (c)(4) (unit 6). That ruling binds only that case, and the IRS's guidance for charities remains in place as of October 2026.

choice.p: Which feature makes an ad that names an incumbent during her campaign less likely to be campaign intervention?
o: It urges her to vote a certain way on a bill that has a floor vote next week
It is paid for by one donor's restricted gift
It runs only in the final week, too briefly to sway many voters
It praises her record, and only negative ads can count as intervention
ow: Who paid for the ad doesn't affect whether its content and timing favor a candidate.
Running close to the election is one of the factors that points toward intervention.
The ban covers support as well as opposition; approving of a candidate's positions is one of the listed factors.

items.p: Match each endorsement by a charity leader to how the IRS treats it.
pairs: CEO's endorsement in an ad the campaign paid for
Allowed: personal speech, with her title listed for identification only
Endorsement in his column in the charity's newsletter
Intervention: an official publication, even though he paid for the column
Board chair urging a vote for X at the annual meeting
Intervention: remarks at an official function speak for the group
Director speaking for a candidate at a campaign rally
Allowed: personal speech at an event the charity doesn't run
items.x: Revenue Ruling 2007-41 says the ban isn't meant to limit leaders 'speaking for themselves,' but 'leaders cannot make partisan comments in official organization publications or at official functions of the organization.' A leader who uses the charity's other assets for a campaign also puts the charity at risk.

units.title: Lobbying
units.desc: What counts as lobbying for a charity, the two ways its limit is measured, and when lobbying triggers federal or state registration.

items.p: In 1966 the Sierra Club, whose donors could deduct their gifts as charitable contributions, ran full-page newspaper ads urging the public to help stop two dams planned for the Grand Canyon. What happened to its tax status?
o: It lost its charity status over lobbying and is now a (c)(4) with a (c)(3) foundation
Nothing: conservation education is a charitable purpose, so the ads were protected as education
It lost tax exemption entirely and has paid income tax like a regular company since then
It was fined for campaign intervention, because the dam fight became an election issue
ow: The ads urged readers to pressure Congress over the dam bills, and the IRS treated that as more lobbying than a charity may do.
It remains tax-exempt today as a social welfare group, which may lobby without limit; gifts to it just aren't deductible.
The ads targeted legislation on the dams and named no candidate, so the issue was lobbying.
keys: it lost its 501(c)(3) charity status because of its lobbying
it now operates as a (c)(4); the Sierra Club Foundation is the separate (c)(3)
items.x: One ad asked: 'Should We Also Flood the Sistine Chapel So Tourists Can Get Nearer the Ceiling?' Neither dam was built. The club became a (c)(4) in 1968; the Sierra Club Foundation is its (c)(3). Since 1976 (section 504), a charity that loses its status for lobbying can't become a (c)(4), so groups set up the (c)(4) in advance. The same limit applies to charities on every side.

items.p: Under a charity's 501(h) lobbying rules, match each communication to how it is classified.
pairs: Email to a senator's aide urging a no vote on a bill
Direct lobbying: to a legislator or staff, on specific legislation, stating a view
Mailer against the bill giving the senator's phone number
Grassroots lobbying: to the public, stating a view, with a call to action
Op-ed against the bill that asks readers to do nothing
Not lobbying under 501(h): a public message with no call to action
Ad urging voters to reject a ballot initiative
Direct lobbying: on a ballot measure, the voters are the legislature
items.x: Treasury Regulation 56.4911-2 defines both kinds. Grassroots lobbying gets its own, smaller limit: a quarter of the charity's total lobbying limit. One wrinkle: a paid mass-media ad on a highly publicized bill, run within two weeks of a vote, is presumed to be grassroots lobbying if it takes a view on the subject and refers to the bill, even without a call to action.

items.p: Under the 501(h) rules, a public message about a bill generally counts as grassroots lobbying only if it includes a 'call to action.' Name two things that count as a call to action.
items.answer: Any two of: telling readers to contact a legislator; giving a legislator's address, phone number or other contact details; providing a petition, postcard or similar way to contact legislators; naming legislators who oppose the bill or are undecided, the reader's own legislator, or members of the committee voting on it.
keys: telling the reader to contact a legislator
giving a legislator's contact details
providing a petition, postcard or similar form
naming opposed or undecided legislators, the reader's legislator, or committee members
items.x: These come from Treasury Regulation 56.4911-2. Under the default 'substantial part' test, the IRS can count advocacy for or against legislation as lobbying even without a call to action, which is one reason charities make the 501(h) election (lesson 2).

choice.p: Which of these turns a charity's public message about a bill into grassroots lobbying under the 501(h) rules?
o: Naming the undecided senators on the committee voting on it
Explaining in detail, with data, why the charity thinks the bill should pass
Citing the bill by name and number and summarizing what it would do
Running it as a paid social media ad instead of a newspaper op-ed
ow: A view is one element, but a public message about a bill with no call to action isn't grassroots lobbying under 501(h).
Referring to specific legislation is required but isn't enough; the message also needs a call to action.
The test is the same in any medium. Only a paid ad on a highly publicized bill shortly before a vote faces an extra presumption.

items.p: A charity drafts a model bill and pitches it to state legislators' staff, though no one has introduced it yet. Under the 501(h) rules, is that lobbying?
o: Yes: a specific proposal the group backs counts even before anyone introduces it
No: lobbying requires a numbered bill, so the clock starts only once the bill is filed
No: offering expert drafting help is technical advice, which the lobbying rules exempt entirely
Only if the charity also runs ads urging the public to back the idea before it is filed
ow: Treasury rules define specific legislation to include a specific proposal the group supports or opposes, introduced or not.
The technical-advice exception covers help given in response to a legislative body's written request. An unrequested pitch doesn't qualify.
Pitching legislators or their staff is direct lobbying by itself; public ads would add grassroots lobbying on top.
keys: yes, it's direct lobbying
specific legislation includes proposals not yet introduced
items.x: Treasury Regulation 56.4911-2 says specific legislation includes 'a specific legislative proposal that the organization either supports or opposes.' Discussing a broad social problem, without addressing a specific proposal, isn't lobbying.

items.p: Many 501(c)(3)s that lobby file the '501(h) election.' Name two ways it changes how their lobbying is limited.
items.answer: It swaps the vague 'no substantial part' test for a dollar limit set by a formula on the group's spending (at most $1 million a year); only money spent counts, so unpaid volunteers' lobbying doesn't; and going over brings a 25% tax on the excess, with exemption at risk only if lobbying normally runs above 150% of the limit.
keys: a clear dollar limit based on spending, at most $1 million
only spending counts; volunteer time doesn't
the penalty is a 25% tax on the excess; exemption is at risk only above 150% of the limit
items.x: Without the election, the IRS judges whether lobbying is 'substantial' from all the facts, with no safe number, and the penalty can be losing exemption. The 501(h) limit is 20% of the first $500,000 of exempt-purpose spending, falling in steps to 5%. At most a quarter of the limit can go to grassroots lobbying (urging the public to contact legislators). Churches and private foundations can't make the election.

choice.p: Which of these is one thing the 501(h) election does for a charity that lobbies?
o: Swaps the vague 'substantial part' test for a dollar limit tied to its spending
Removes all limits on its lobbying, as long as the group reports it to Congress
Lets the group endorse candidates who sponsor the bills it is lobbying for
Exempts all state lobbying, so only lobbying of Congress counts toward the limit
ow: The election replaces a vague limit with a dollar limit. Lobbying reports to Congress come from a separate law.
Nothing changes the ban on supporting or opposing candidates.
Lobbying on legislation counts at the federal, state and local levels, including ballot measures.

items.p: A charity that hasn't made the 501(h) election does its lobbying almost entirely through unpaid volunteers and spends little money on it. Why could it still have a problem?
o: The default test weighs volunteers' time as well as spending, and it sets no safe number
Volunteers who lobby must register as federal lobbyists, and the charity is fined if they don't
The default test caps lobbying at 5% of the budget, and volunteer hours are valued at market wages
It owes the 25% excise tax on any lobbying above its limit, whether done by volunteers or staff
ow: Federal registration covers paid lobbyists who meet time and spending tests (lesson 3); unpaid volunteers don't trigger it.
The default test has no fixed percentage; the IRS weighs all the facts. A 5% tax applies only after a charity loses exemption for lobbying.
The 25% tax applies only to charities that made the 501(h) election. Under the default test the main risk is losing exemption.
keys: the substantial part test counts volunteer time as well as spending
no bright line, and the penalty can be loss of exemption
items.x: The IRS says it weighs 'the time devoted (by both compensated and volunteer workers)' along with spending. Under the 501(h) election only money counts, so a volunteer-heavy group can gain a lot from electing. A charity that loses exemption for lobbying also owes a 5% tax on that year's lobbying spending, and managers who agreed knowing the risk can owe 5% too.

items.p: Under the 501(h) rules, match each charity activity to the reason it isn't counted as lobbying.
pairs: Report that takes a side on a bill but sets out facts fairly
Nonpartisan analysis: a full and fair treatment, with no direct call to action
Testimony given at a committee's written request
Technical advice requested in writing by a legislative body
Meeting legislators on a bill to end its own exemption
Self-defense: legislation affecting the group's existence, powers or tax status
Comments to an agency on a proposed regulation
Agencies don't make legislation, so it falls outside the definition
Public forum on the causes of child poverty
Discussion of a broad social problem, with no specific proposal
items.x: These come from section 4911 and Treasury Regulation 56.4911-2. The self-defense exception covers the charity's own contacts with legislators; urging the public to call about the same bill is still grassroots lobbying. Nonpartisan analysis can become grassroots lobbying if the charity later sends it out with a call to action. Agency work can still count under the federal lobbyist registration law (lesson 3).

items.p: A nonprofit's policy director spends about a quarter of her time on federal lobbying, including meetings with several Senate offices. The group expects about $25,000 in lobbying costs this quarter. Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act, what must it do?
o: Register with the House and Senate within 45 days, then file a report every quarter
Nothing, because charities with the 501(h) election are exempt from registering
Register only if it also hires an outside lobbying firm to contact Congress for it
Report the lobbying on its Form 990, which satisfies the federal registration law
ow: The 501(h) election is a tax rule. It doesn't exempt anyone from the separate federal registration law.
In-house lobbying counts: a group registers once an employee meets the lobbyist test and its lobbying costs top $16,000 a quarter.
The Form 990 goes to the IRS. Registration (LD-1) and quarterly reports (LD-2) go to the Clerk of the House and Secretary of the Senate.
keys: register (LD-1) with the House Clerk and Senate Secretary within 45 days
then file quarterly activity reports (LD-2)
items.x: A lobbyist is a paid employee who makes more than one lobbying contact and spends 20% or more of her time on lobbying activities, which include research and planning for contacts. Since January 1, 2025, a group lobbying with its own staff registers once those costs exceed $16,000 a quarter ($3,500 per client for outside firms). Reports are due 20 days after each quarter, quiet ones included, until the group files a termination. Lobbyists also file twice-yearly reports on their political contributions.

items.p: Federal tax rules and the Lobbying Disclosure Act (LDA) define lobbying differently. Match each activity by a charity to how the two laws treat it.
pairs: Meeting a White House aide about a draft executive order
Counts under the LDA only: covered executive officials are included
Ad urging the public to call senators about a bill
Counts under tax rules only: messages to the public aren't LDA contacts
Meeting a senator's staff to urge a yes vote on a bill
Counts under both laws
Comment filed in an agency's public rulemaking docket
Counts under neither law
items.x: LDA lobbying contacts cover legislation, rules, executive orders, federal programs and nominations, made to covered officials such as members of Congress and their staff, White House staff and political appointees; most career staff aren't covered. Charity tax rules count only work on legislation, including grassroots calls to action. Charities can report LDA expenses using their IRS figures, but the two definitions still differ.

items.p: A nonprofit registered under the federal lobbying law starts pressing New York state legislators on a bill. What does it need to know about registration?
o: New York has its own registration, required once lobbying pay and costs top $5,000 a year
Nothing new: its federal registration also covers lobbying of state legislatures
Nothing: state lobbying laws cover businesses and their hired firms, and nonprofits are exempt
New York accepts the group's 501(h) election in place of a state registration
ow: The LDA covers federal officials only; states run their own registration systems.
New York's law covers nonprofits that lobby above its threshold like any other organization.
The 501(h) election sets federal tax limits and has no effect on state lobbying registration.
keys: state lobbying registration is separate from federal registration
New York requires it once lobbying compensation and expenses exceed $5,000 in a calendar year
items.x: New York's Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government requires registration once combined lobbying compensation and expenses at the state and municipal level exceed, or are expected to exceed, $5,000 in a calendar year (instructions revised May 2026). Thresholds and definitions vary by state, and New York City has its own rules too, so check each place you lobby.

units.title: (c)(4)s
units.desc: How much election work a social welfare group can do, the taxes and notices that come with politics and lobbying, and how private its donors are.

items.p: A (c)(4) applied for IRS recognition in 2011 and was turned down in 2020 under the IRS's test for how much political activity is too much. It sued. In September 2025, what did a federal court in Washington decide about that test?
o: The IRS's test was too vague to apply to the group; the court sought a new standard
The test was valid, since the IRS may weigh all the facts and circumstances of each case together
The court replaced the test with a bright line: political spending must stay under 50%
The court struck the limit for all (c)(4)s, which may now do unlimited election work
ow: The court held the multi-factor test too vague for rules touching speech, since applicants can't tell how the factors are weighed.
The court rejected the standards both sides proposed and ordered more briefing; it adopted no percentage.
The ruling binds only that case. For other groups the existing facts-and-circumstances approach still applies.
keys: the IRS's test was unconstitutionally vague as applied to that group
the court set no replacement yet, and the ruling binds only that case
items.x: Freedom Path v. IRS (D.D.C.), decided as applied to that group. The court said the IRS gives no guidance on how to weigh the factors against one another, and that sending the case back would not work because a spending-bill rider bars the IRS from writing new (c)(4) standards. It heard argument on the parties' proposed standards on May 12, 2026; as of October 2026 no ruling had been reported. The test applies to (c)(4)s on every side.

items.p: How much election work (supporting or opposing candidates) may a 501(c)(4) do?
o: Some, as long as it isn't the group's primary activity; no exact percentage is set
Up to 49% of its total spending, a cap written into the Treasury regulations
None at all: like a 501(c)(3), it may never support or oppose a candidate
Any amount at all, as long as it doesn't coordinate with the candidates it supports
ow: No regulation sets a percentage. Lawyers debate whether 'primary' means more than half; Alliance for Justice advises keeping political spending under 30 to 40 percent to be cautious.
The IRS says a (c)(4) 'may engage in some political activities, so long as that is not its primary activity.'
That describes a super PAC. A (c)(4) whose main activity is elections risks its exemption.
keys: allowed, but it can't be the group's primary activity
no fixed percentage in the rules
items.x: The IRS weighs all the facts and circumstances, so groups keep a margin. Lobbying on issues tied to the group's mission doesn't count as political activity and can be its main activity. A (c)(4)'s political spending is also taxed under section 527(f), on the lesser of that spending or the group's net investment income. For more election work, a (c)(4) can set up its own PAC funded by separate contributions; money the (c)(4) itself gives a super PAC is still taxable political spending under 527(f).

items.p: Why hasn't the IRS issued clearer rules on how much political activity a (c)(4) may do?
items.answer: Congress has blocked it. A rider attached to federal spending laws since December 2015, including the fiscal 2026 law, bars Treasury and the IRS from issuing any new regulation, ruling or general guidance on the (c)(4) social welfare standard, and keeps the standard that was in effect on January 1, 2010.
keys: a rider in federal appropriations (spending) laws bars new (c)(4) guidance
the standard in effect on January 1, 2010 stays in place
items.x: The rider bars any 'regulation, revenue ruling, or other guidance not limited to a particular taxpayer' on the social welfare standard, including rules the IRS proposed in 2013. It first appeared in the December 2015 spending law and is in the fiscal 2026 law (P.L. 119-75); the stopgap funding the government to December 11, 2026 continues fiscal 2026 'authority and conditions.' It is why the Freedom Path court couldn't simply send the case back to the IRS.

choice.p: Why hasn't the IRS issued clearer rules on how much political activity a (c)(4) may do?
o: A rider in federal spending laws bars it from issuing new (c)(4) standards
The Supreme Court held in 2014 that only Congress may define political activity
The tax code itself sets the limit at 49% of spending, so only Congress can change it
Election spending rules belong to the FEC, so the IRS has no power to write them
ow: No such ruling exists. The obstacle is a rider Congress attached to its spending laws.
The statute says 'exclusively,' the IRS's regulation reads that as 'primarily,' and neither sets a percentage.
The FEC regulates campaign finance; whether a group qualifies for tax exemption is the IRS's job.

items.p: Three weeks before a senator's reelection, a (c)(4) runs TV ads praising her stand on gun policy, an issue that divides her race. The ads aren't tied to any pending bill or vote. How would the IRS likely treat the cost?
o: As political spending: it counts toward the primary-activity limit and may face the 527(f) tax
As lobbying, since gun policy is legislation, so the (c)(4) may spend on it without limit
As social welfare education, since the ads praise her record and never tell anyone how to vote
As an in-kind contribution to her campaign, which the (c)(4) must report to the FEC as a gift
ow: Lobbying needs a link to legislation. An ad praising a candidate before her election, tied to no bill or vote, fits the IRS's political factors.
An express call to vote isn't required, and praise counts as much as criticism. Naming a candidate near her election on a dividing issue can be enough.
Unless the ad was coordinated with the campaign, it isn't a contribution to it. FEC disclosure for uncoordinated ads is covered in unit 7.
keys: political (exempt-function) spending
counts toward the primary-activity limit and may be taxed under 527(f)
