items.x: Revenue Ruling 2004-6 uses factors much like those for charities (unit 4): naming a candidate, timing near an election, targeting voters in that race and an issue that sets the candidates apart point toward political spending; tying the ad to a scheduled vote or an ongoing series points away. The Freedom Path court found this test too vague as applied to that group, but practitioners report the IRS still applies the same approach to others.

items.p: This year a (c)(4) spends $300,000 on ads backing candidates and earns $10,000 in investment income. What does the section 527(f) tax come to, roughly?
o: 21% of $10,000: the tax hits the lesser of investment income and political spending
21% of $300,000, because all of a (c)(4)'s political spending is taxed at the corporate rate
Nothing, because a (c)(4) is tax-exempt and its political spending is legal within limits
25% of whatever its political spending exceeds 49% of its total budget for the year
ow: The taxable amount can't exceed the group's net investment income, which here is far smaller.
Exemption doesn't shield political spending: section 527(f) taxes it, up to the group's net investment income.
That mixes up the 25% tax on charities' excess lobbying with the (c)(4) rules, and no 49% line appears in the law.
keys: tax on the lesser of net investment income or political spending
at the 21% top corporate rate: about $2,100 here
items.x: Section 527(f) adds the smaller amount to the group's taxable income and taxes it at the top corporate rate, 21%. A (c)(4) with no investment income owes nothing. Lobbying on legislation isn't covered by 527(f); member dues spent on lobbying trigger a separate notice rule.

items.p: A (c)(4) wants to do more to help elect federal candidates. Give two reasons lawyers often suggest doing that work through a PAC the (c)(4) sets up.
items.answer: Federal law bars corporations, including nonprofit (c)(4)s, from giving to federal candidates, so direct contributions need a PAC funded by voluntary gifts. And money the PAC raises and spends isn't the (c)(4)'s own political spending, so the (c)(4) can avoid the 527(f) tax on it.
keys: corporations, including (c)(4)s, can't give to federal candidates, but a PAC funded by voluntary gifts can
the PAC is a separate organization for tax purposes, so its spending avoids the (c)(4)'s 527(f) tax
items.x: Under section 527(f)(3), the PAC (a 'separate segregated fund') is a separate organization for tax purposes, and contributions passed to it promptly and directly don't count as the (c)(4)'s political spending. Alliance for Justice notes a (c)(4) 'may avoid the 527(f) tax altogether' this way. Who a connected PAC may ask for money is covered in unit 7.

choice.p: Which is one reason a (c)(4) runs candidate-support work through its own PAC?
o: Federal law bars corporations, including (c)(4)s, from giving to federal candidates
Gifts to a PAC are tax-deductible for donors, unlike gifts to the (c)(4) itself
PAC donors are never disclosed to anyone, so the PAC protects donors' privacy better
PACs face no federal limits on what they can give to a candidate's campaign
ow: Gifts to political organizations, PACs included, aren't deductible either.
Federal PACs must name donors who give more than $200 in a calendar year on their FEC reports, so a PAC offers less privacy.
A traditional PAC faces contribution limits, such as $5,000 per election to a candidate for a multicandidate PAC.

items.p: Why does the tax code push a (c)(4) whose members are mostly businesses to tell them what share of their dues went to lobbying?
items.answer: Businesses can't deduct lobbying or political costs, and the tax code stops them from deducting those costs through dues. The group must tell members what share of dues went to lobbying and political activity, which they can't deduct, or else pay a 'proxy tax' at the top corporate rate on that spending.
keys: businesses can't deduct lobbying and political costs (section 162(e))
the group must give members a notice of the nondeductible share, or pay a proxy tax on the spending
items.x: Section 162(e) bars business deductions for lobbying and political spending, and section 6033(e) applies that to dues. It doesn't apply to groups whose only such spending is in-house lobbying of $2,000 or less, or to groups that show almost all their dues are nondeductible anyway (for example, over 90% comes from members paying small dues, or from charities). (c)(3)s are outside this rule.

choice.p: Why does the tax code push a (c)(4) with business members to tell them what share of dues went to lobbying?
o: So they don't deduct lobbying costs through dues; otherwise the group pays a proxy tax
Because its lobbying is capped at a quarter of its budget, as under 501(h)
Because each member business must register as a lobbyist under the federal LDA
Because members' dues become taxable income to the group once it lobbies at all
ow: A (c)(4) has no lobbying cap, and the 501(h) limits apply only to charities that elect them.
LDA duties fall on whoever employs or retains the lobbyists, which here is the (c)(4) itself.
The rule is about members' deductions: the group either sends the notice or pays the proxy tax.

items.p: A (c)(4) that lobbies Congress wants to apply for a federal grant to run a job-training program. What stands in its way?
o: A federal law makes (c)(4)s that lobby ineligible for federal grants, awards and loans
Nothing, as long as it keeps the grant in a separate account and spends none of it on lobbying
It must first make the 501(h) election, which shows the IRS its lobbying stays within limits
Only (c)(3) charities may receive federal money of any kind, from grants to contracts
ow: Separating the money isn't enough: a (c)(4) that engages in lobbying is ineligible for grants altogether.
Only (c)(3) charities can make the 501(h) election, and it wouldn't affect this bar.
The bar covers only (c)(4)s that lobby, and only grants, awards and loans; a 1996 change dropped contracts.
keys: a (c)(4) that engages in lobbying can't receive federal grants, awards or loans (2 U.S.C. 1611)
it applies even if the grant itself isn't used for lobbying
items.x: The rule sits in the Lobbying Disclosure Act at 2 U.S.C. 1611 and turns on whether the (c)(4) engages in lobbying activities as that law defines them, which means federal lobbying. It names only (c)(4)s, so a group's (c)(3) affiliate falls outside it.

items.p: An FEC rule let nonprofits that ran independent ads for or against federal candidates name only donors who gave for a specific ad. A watchdog group sued. What did a federal court decide in 2018?
o: It threw the rule out: donors giving over $200 for political purposes must now be named
It upheld the rule, holding that the First Amendment protects nonprofit donors' privacy
It required nonprofits that run such ads to name every donor over $200, whatever the gift's purpose
It barred nonprofits from paying for independent ads unless they first register as PACs
ow: The court held the rule conflicted with the broader disclosure the statute requires, and an appeals court agreed in 2020.
Gifts made for political purposes, including to fund any independent ad, must be reported; gifts with no political purpose generally aren't.
Nonprofits can still pay for independent ads without becoming PACs. They report them to the FEC on Form 5.
keys: the court threw out the narrow FEC rule
groups making independent expenditures must name donors of more than $200 given for political purposes
items.x: CREW v. FEC (D.D.C. 2018), affirmed in 2020. Since September 18, 2018, a group spending more than $250 a year on independent expenditures must report each donor who gave over $200 for political purposes, flagging gifts 'made for the purpose of furthering any independent expenditure.' Unit 7 covers independent expenditures themselves.

items.p: A donor gives $500,000 to a (c)(4) for general support, with no political purpose. Later the group spends part of its budget on independent ads. Under federal rules, where must the donor's name appear?
o: Only in the group's own records, which it must give the IRS on request
On the public copy of the group's Form 990, since the gift is over $5,000
On the group's FEC report, since part of its budget paid for independent ads
On its Schedule B filed with the IRS, which the IRS keeps confidential
ow: A (c)(4)'s public 990 doesn't show donor names, and (c)(4)s no longer list names on their IRS filing at all.
FEC reports reach gifts made for political purposes; a gift with no such purpose generally isn't reported.
Since 2020, (c)(4)s enter 'N/A' for donor names on Schedule B. Only (c)(3)s and 527s list them.
keys: no public filing names the donor
the (c)(4) must keep the name and give it to the IRS on request
items.x: Schedule B instructions (revised December 2024) tell groups other than (c)(3)s and 527s to collect donor names and addresses and 'Make the information available to the IRS upon request.' Under the 2018 CREW ruling, the FEC question is whether the gift was made for political purposes. Unit 10 covers other ways donors can be exposed.

items.p: A wealthy donor gives $5 million to a (c)(4) that lobbies on climate policy. What are the federal tax consequences for the donor?
o: No income tax deduction, and no gift tax, because a 2015 law exempted gifts to (c)(4)s
An income tax deduction like a gift to a charity, since the group works for the common good
Gift tax on everything above the annual exclusion, as for a large gift to a person
No deduction, and gift tax only on whatever part the (c)(4) spends on elections
ow: The IRS says gifts to (c)(4)s generally aren't deductible as charitable contributions.
Before 2015 this was an open question, and the IRS briefly audited five (c)(4) donors in 2011; a 2015 law settled it.
The exemption covers any gift to an exempt (c)(4) for its use, whatever the group then spends it on.
keys: no charitable income tax deduction
no gift tax: gifts to (c)(4)s have been exempt since December 2015
items.x: Section 2501(a)(6), added in December 2015, exempts gifts to (c)(4), (c)(5) and (c)(6) groups. Before that, the IRS opened gift tax audits of five (c)(4) donors in 2011, then closed them within months and suspended enforcement. Gifts to PACs and other political organizations have their own gift tax exemption.

units.title: Campaign finance basics
units.desc: Who may give to federal campaigns and how much, when outside spending counts as 'coordinated', and the kinds of PAC an advocacy group can run.

items.p: After the crypto exchange FTX collapsed in 2022, it emerged that its executives had given tens of millions of dollars to candidates and PACs in their own names, though the money really came from the company or its founder. How did federal prosecutors treat these gifts?
o: As crimes: an executive pleaded guilty to conspiracy to make unlawful contributions and was imprisoned
As civil matters for the FEC, since campaign-finance violations are punished with fines, never prison
As lawful, because each executive stayed under the per-election limit for every candidate
As lawful wherever the money went to super PACs, since those may take unlimited sums from anyone
ow: Knowing and willful violations are federal crimes; giving more than $10,000 a year in another's name can bring up to two years in prison, or five at $25,000 or more.
Staying under the limit doesn't help: the law bans any contribution made in another person's name, because it hides the real donor.
The ban on giving in another's name covers contributions to every kind of political committee, super PACs included.
keys: prosecuted as crimes
gifts made in the names of straw donors or paid with corporate money
items.x: Ryan Salame, an FTX executive, pleaded guilty to conspiring to make unlawful political contributions and defraud the FEC (and to running an unlicensed money-transmitting business) and was sentenced in May 2024 to 90 months. DOJ said he and others made over 300 gifts that were unlawful because they were 'made in the name of a straw donor or paid for with corporate funds.' The lasting rule (52 U.S.C. 30122) binds donors and committees of every party: no one may give in another's name, let their name be used, or knowingly accept such a gift.

items.p: Three people each offer $1,000 to a US Senate candidate: a US citizen living in Paris, a Canadian with a green card living in Ohio, and a German citizen working in Ohio on an H-1B visa. Who may legally give?
o: The US citizen and the green-card holder, but not the visa holder
All three, because the ban reaches only people who live abroad
Only the US citizen, since only citizens may give to federal candidates
Only the two who live in Ohio, since US residence decides who may give
ow: Residence doesn't matter: anyone who is neither a citizen nor a lawful permanent resident is a foreign national, wherever they live.
Lawful permanent residents (green-card holders) are not foreign nationals and may give like citizens.
Citizenship or permanent residence decides, so the citizen in Paris may give and the visa holder in Ohio may not.
keys: the citizen and the green-card holder may give
the visa holder is a foreign national and may not
items.x: Foreign nationals (anyone who is neither a citizen nor a lawful permanent resident, plus foreign governments, parties and companies) may not give or spend in connection with any federal, state or local election. They also may not take part in an organization's decisions about election spending, so a (c)(4) or PAC with a foreign-national board member keeps that person out of those decisions. The FEC expects recipients to ask questions when they see a foreign passport, address or bank.

items.p: A consultant works as a sole proprietor and holds a contract with a federal agency. May she give $1,000 of her own money to a House candidate while the contract is in effect?
o: No: as an individual contractor, she may not give even from personal funds
Yes: the contractor ban covers only business funds, so her personal money is fine
Yes: the ban applies only to contractor corporations, which can't give to candidates anyway
Yes, as long as the candidate has no role in overseeing her agency or its contracts
ow: For individuals and sole proprietors, the FEC says the ban covers 'any funds (business or personal) under their control.'
Corporations were already barred, so the contractor rule matters most for individuals, partnerships and some LLCs.
The ban doesn't depend on any link between candidate and contract; it covers every federal candidate, party and committee.
keys: no, not even from personal funds
the ban covers individual and sole-proprietor federal contractors
items.x: The ban (52 U.S.C. 30119) runs from the start of contract negotiations until the work is done or talks end, and covers gifts to any federal party, committee or candidate; it doesn't reach state or local races. The FEC has fined contractors for giving to super PACs, though Covington's lawyers argue NRSC v. FEC (2026) casts doubt on that. A contractor's spouse and a contracting company's employees may give their own money, and a contractor corporation may still run a connected PAC. The en banc D.C. Circuit unanimously upheld the ban for individuals in Wagner v. FEC (2015).

items.p: Federal law bars corporations, including nonprofit corporations like most 501(c)(4)s, from giving to federal candidates. Does that ban stop a (c)(4) from giving to a candidate for state legislature?
o: No: state law decides, and states range from banning corporate gifts to allowing unlimited ones
Yes: the federal corporate ban covers candidates for every office, whether federal, state or local
No, and no state may stop it either, since Citizens United protects corporate political giving
Yes, unless the (c)(4) first routes the money through a super PAC registered in that state
ow: The corporate ban in 52 U.S.C. 30118 covers federal elections (only national banks and federally chartered corporations are barred from all races). The foreign-national ban, by contrast, does reach state and local races.
Citizens United protected independent spending; it left contribution bans in place, and many states ban corporate contributions.
Super PACs can't give to candidates, and whether the (c)(4) may give directly turns on that state's own law.
keys: no, the federal ban covers only federal elections
state law governs; some states ban corporate contributions and others allow them
items.x: NCSL's July 2025 overview counted 23 states that completely prohibit corporate contributions to state campaigns and five (Alabama, Nebraska, Oregon, Utah and Virginia) that allowed unlimited ones. States also set their own limits, registration and reporting rules, so a group active in state races needs advice on each state. Bolder Advocacy notes that many states let (c)(4)s create connected state PACs.

items.p: In NRSC v. FEC, the National Republican Senatorial Committee challenged federal caps on how much a political party may spend in coordination with its own candidates. How did the Supreme Court rule in June 2026?
o: It struck down the caps, so parties may spend without limit in coordination with their candidates
It upheld the caps, saying parties could otherwise act as conduits for donors to get around limits
It struck down coordination limits for every spender, so super PACs may now work with campaigns
It struck down the limits on how much individuals may give to party committees each year
ow: That was the reasoning of the 2001 Colorado II decision upholding the caps, which NRSC overruled.
The ruling covered only parties. Outside groups such as super PACs and (c)(4)s still may not coordinate.
Limits on giving to parties and candidates were left unchanged; an individual may still give a national party up to $44,300 a year (2025-2026).
keys: struck down the limits on party coordinated spending
parties may now coordinate spending with their candidates without limit
items.x: Justice Kavanaugh wrote for a 6-3 Court, which held the party limits violate the First Amendment and overruled Colorado II; the ruling covers every party's committees. The lasting rule for everyone else is unchanged: when a PAC, super PAC or nonprofit coordinates spending with a campaign, the spending counts as a contribution to that campaign, subject to its limits and source bans. Covington's lawyers said the reasoning calls other limits into question, such as caps on party contributions to candidates.

items.p: A super PAC's director has coffee with a Senate campaign's manager, who explains which counties worry the campaign most. Two months before the election, the super PAC buys TV ads in those counties attacking the opponent. The manager never asked for ads. What is the legal problem?
o: They count as coordinated, making them an in-kind contribution far over the limits
None, because the campaign never asked for the ads or agreed to anything about them
None, as long as the ads only criticize the opponent's record and never urge a vote
The super PAC must now register as an agent of the campaign and file its ads with it
ow: FEC rules need no request or agreement: a substantial discussion of the campaign's plans or needs that is material to the ads is enough.
Ads naming a Senate candidate within 90 days of the election, aimed at that state's voters, meet the FEC's content test even without 'vote against' wording.
There is no such registration; the consequence of coordination is that the spending is treated as a contribution.
keys: the ads are coordinated communications
treated as an in-kind contribution to the campaign
a substantial discussion of campaign plans is enough; no request needed
items.x: Under 11 CFR 109.21, an ad is coordinated if an outsider pays for it, it meets a content test, and it meets a conduct test: a request or suggestion, the campaign's material involvement, a substantial discussion, or a shared vendor or former staffer (within 120 days) passing on private campaign information. Information the campaign has made public doesn't count, and a written firewall that actually works gives shared vendors a safe harbor.

items.p: Forty-five days before the general election, a 501(c)(4) spends $200,000 on statewide TV ads criticizing Senator Reyes, who is up for reelection, for a vote on a bill. The ads urge viewers to call her office and never say how to vote. How does federal election law treat them?
o: As electioneering communications, which the group must report to the FEC within 24 hours
As independent expenditures, because they criticize a candidate shortly before her election
As pure lobbying, outside FEC rules, because they never ask anyone to vote against her
As illegal, because corporations may not pay for TV ads naming candidates near an election
ow: An independent expenditure needs express advocacy, such as 'vote against Reyes'; these ads have none.
Lobbying content doesn't exempt them: a TV ad naming a federal candidate within 60 days of the general election, aimed at her voters, is an electioneering communication.
Citizens United (2010) struck down that ban; the ads are legal but must be disclosed.
keys: electioneering communications
reported to the FEC within 24 hours once spending tops $10,000 in a year
items.x: An electioneering communication is a broadcast, cable or satellite ad that names a federal candidate, runs within 60 days before a general election or 30 before a primary, and can reach 50,000 or more people in the candidate's state or district. Once a group's spending on them tops $10,000 in a year, it reports within 24 hours, and again each time it spends another $10,000. The same message as a mailer or online ad would not be one. For a (c)(3), ads like these also raise the campaign-intervention question covered in the unit on (c)(3)s and elections.

items.p: Match each kind of election-related spending to what defines it under federal rules.
pairs: Independent expenditure
Ad expressly urging a vote for or against a candidate, made without the campaign's involvement
Electioneering communication
TV or radio ad naming a federal candidate shortly before an election, aimed at their voters
Coordinated communication
Ad an outside group pays for after the campaign requests it or shares its plans, so it counts as a contribution
In-kind contribution
Goods or services given to a campaign free or below the usual price, such as a mailing list
items.x: The label decides what's allowed and what's reported. Corporations, including (c)(4)s, may make independent expenditures and electioneering communications (and must disclose them), but may not give federal candidates contributions, in cash or in kind. FEC rules list 'membership lists, and mailing lists' among things of value, so lending a campaign your list for free is a contribution.

items.p: Match each recipient to the most one individual may give it under federal limits for 2025-2026.
pairs: A House candidate
$3,500 per election, with the primary and general counted separately
A traditional PAC
$5,000 per calendar year
A national party committee's main account
$44,300 per calendar year
A super PAC
No limit
items.x: So a donor may give a House candidate $7,000 across the primary and general. The candidate and party limits rise with inflation in odd-numbered years; the $5,000 PAC limit is fixed. National parties may also keep additional accounts with limits of $132,900 each per year. A PAC founder's math starts here: no one donor can give a traditional PAC more than $5,000 a year.

items.p: A 501(c)(4) sets up a connected PAC (a 'separate segregated fund') to give to federal candidates. Who may the PAC ask for contributions, and who may pay its rent, salaries and fundraising costs?
items.answer: It may solicit its 'restricted class' (for a membership group, its members plus its salaried managers and executives, and their families), never the general public. The (c)(4) may pay the PAC's setup, administration and fundraising costs from its own treasury, with no dollar limit and no FEC reporting.
keys: only the restricted class (members, executive and administrative staff, their families)
not the general public
the (c)(4) may pay the PAC's overhead from its treasury, unlimited and unreported
items.x: Federal law carves a sponsor's costs of setting up, running and fundraising for its own PAC out of the corporate contribution ban. The PAC may also send two written appeals a year to the sponsor's other employees. Bolder Advocacy notes that running a (c)(4)'s candidate work through a connected PAC can spare the (c)(4) the section 527(f) tax on political spending. The PAC's name must include the sponsor's full name, though it may also use a well-known acronym.

choice.p: Which describes the fundraising and overhead rules for a (c)(4)'s connected PAC?
o: Only members and salaried managers may be asked; the (c)(4) may pay its overhead without limit
It may ask the general public for gifts; the (c)(4) may cover its overhead up to $5,000 a year
It may ask anyone for gifts, but must pay all its overhead from the contributions it raises
It may ask only members for gifts, and the (c)(4) must report each overhead payment as a contribution
ow: A connected PAC may not solicit the general public, and the sponsor's payment of its overhead has no dollar cap.
That describes a nonconnected PAC. A connected PAC's sponsor may pay its costs, but its solicitations are limited.
Overhead paid by the sponsor isn't a contribution and isn't reported to the FEC.

items.p: Why might an advocacy group's founders set up a nonconnected PAC instead of a PAC connected to their (c)(4)?
o: It may solicit the general public, though it must cover its own overhead
It may give unlimited amounts to candidates, since no corporation sponsors it
It may use corporate contributions to fund its gifts to federal candidates
It need not report its donors to the FEC, unlike a PAC tied to a sponsor
ow: Every traditional PAC faces the same caps on gifts to candidates, such as $5,000 per election for a multicandidate PAC.
Money given to candidates must come from permitted sources; corporate money can go only to a super PAC or a hybrid PAC's separate account.
Both kinds itemize donors who give more than $200 a year in their FEC reports.
keys: it can solicit the general public
it must pay its own overhead; no sponsor pays it
items.x: The tradeoff runs both ways. A connected PAC gets free overhead from its sponsor but may ask only its restricted class; a nonconnected PAC may raise from anyone but pays rent, staff and fundraising out of capped contributions. A sponsor that isn't a corporation or union may help a nonconnected PAC, but that help counts as a contribution, subject to limits and disclosure.

items.p: A 'hybrid PAC' gives to candidates and also takes unlimited contributions, including from corporations. What must it do to keep both activities legal?
o: Keep two bank accounts: capped money for candidates, unlimited money for independent ads
Disclose its unlimited donors within 24 hours, which then lets it use their money for candidate gifts
Spend its unlimited money only on issue ads that avoid naming any federal candidate
Cap each donor's unlimited gifts at $5,000 for every candidate the PAC supports
ow: Disclosure doesn't change the source rules: unlimited or corporate money may never fund contributions to candidates.
The unlimited account exists to pay for independent ads, which may name candidates and urge votes for or against them.
There's no per-candidate cap on the unlimited account; its money simply can't go to candidates.
keys: two separate bank accounts
capped, permitted money for candidate contributions
unlimited money only for independent spending
items.x: Hybrid PACs date from Carey v. FEC (2011), after which the FEC stopped enforcing limits on gifts to a PAC's separate 'non-contribution account.' Each account pays a share of overhead that 'closely corresponds' to its share of activity. A super PAC is simpler to run but can't give to candidates at all.

units.title: Running affiliated groups
units.desc: How a (c)(3), a (c)(4) and a PAC work as one family without letting tax-deductible money pay for lobbying or politics.

lessons.title: Why advocacy groups come in families

items.p: A nonprofit called Taxation With Representation argued that the limit on lobbying by tax-deductible charities violated the First Amendment. In Regan v. Taxation With Representation (1983), what did the Supreme Court decide?
o: It upheld the limit, partly because the group could lobby through a (c)(4) affiliate
It struck down the limit, holding that lobbying is protected speech the tax code may not burden
It upheld the limit and also barred charities from running affiliates that lobby
It struck down the limit for charities whose lobbying is nonpartisan and tied to their mission
ow: The Court reaffirmed its earlier holding that 'Congress is not required by the First Amendment to subsidize lobbying,' including through deductible gifts.
The opposite: the ruling assumed the group could lobby through a (c)(4) affiliate, as it had in the past.
The Court upheld the limit as written and carved out no exception for mission-related lobbying.
keys: upheld the lobbying limit
Congress need not subsidize lobbying
the group could lobby through a (c)(4) affiliate
items.x: The Court said the group could get deductible gifts for non-lobbying work by 'returning to the dual structure it used in the past,' but would 'have to ensure that the § 501(c)(3) organization did not subsidize the § 501(c)(4) organization.' A footnote said the IRS 'apparently requires only that the two groups be separately incorporated and keep records adequate' to show deductible gifts don't pay for lobbying. That is the legal basis for today's (c)(3)/(c)(4) families.

items.p: A group is setting up a 501(c)(3) and a sister 501(c)(4). Can the same people sit on both boards?
o: Yes, even identical boards are allowed, if each meets and decides for its own group
No: the IRS treats shared directors as merging the two groups into a single organization
Yes, but no more than half of either board may also serve on the other group's board
Yes, but the (c)(3) may have no say at all over who sits on the (c)(4)'s board
ow: The IRS routinely recognizes (c)(3)/(c)(4) pairs with complete or partial board overlap; the risk comes from mixing money and decisions.
Tax law sets no such cap, though practitioners differ on how much overlap is wise.
A (c)(3) may control its (c)(4) affiliate, including choosing its board; the (c)(4) still runs its own day-to-day work.
keys: yes, overlapping or identical boards are allowed
each board meets separately and acts for its own organization
items.x: Directors owe fiduciary duties to each organization separately, so practice guides such as Adler & Colvin's advise separate meetings, minutes and records, with each board deciding transactions between the two. Venable notes that many groups, as a precaution, avoid seating a majority of the same people on both boards; tax law doesn't require that.

items.p: The founders of a 501(c)(3) research group want a PAC that gives to federal candidates. What structure lets them have one?
o: A (c)(4) affiliate sponsors the PAC and pays its costs, which the (c)(3) can't
The (c)(3) sponsors the PAC directly, as long as no deductible gifts pay its costs
The (c)(3) sets up the PAC but gives it a board fully separate from the charity's
The (c)(3) collects its donors' checks for the PAC and forwards them to it
ow: A (c)(3) may not set up or pay for a PAC at all, whatever money it uses; that is campaign intervention.
A separate board doesn't help; the (c)(3) still can't create or fund a political committee.
Collecting and forwarding PAC checks is a free service to a political committee, and a (c)(3) may not give support of any kind to political organizations.
keys: a (c)(4) affiliate sponsors the connected PAC
the (c)(3) can't sponsor or fund a PAC
items.x: Bolder Advocacy's comparison chart lists establishing and paying for a connected PAC as off-limits for a (c)(3) and allowed for a (c)(4). Adler & Colvin warn that a (c)(4) with little activity of its own, set up mainly as a platform for its (c)(3)'s PAC, invites the IRS to call the arrangement an artifice. Each layer does more politics with money that carries fewer tax benefits: gifts to the (c)(4) and the PAC aren't deductible.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) that has made the 501(h) election gives its sister (c)(4) a $50,000 grant with no strings attached. The (c)(4) spends heavily on lobbying. How is the grant treated?
o: As the (c)(3)'s own lobbying spending, up to the amount the (c)(4) spends on lobbying
As an ordinary charitable grant, since only the (c)(4)'s own rules govern how it spends money
As campaign activity that automatically costs the (c)(3) its tax exemption
As a prohibited transfer, since a (c)(3) may never give money to a (c)(4)
ow: Treasury rules look through an unrestricted grant to a lobbying non-charity and count it against the (c)(3)'s own lobbying limits.
Lobbying and campaign activity are separate categories; the grant uses up the (c)(3)'s lobbying room, which it may have to spare.
A (c)(3) may fund a (c)(4), either restricted to a non-lobbying charitable project or counted as its own lobbying.
keys: counts as the (c)(3)'s own lobbying expenditure
up to what the (c)(4) spends on lobbying
items.x: Under Treasury rules for electing charities, a below-value transfer to a non-charity that lobbies counts as the charity's own lobbying: first as grassroots lobbying, up to the recipient's grassroots spending, then as direct lobbying, up to its direct lobbying. A 'controlled grant,' limited to a specific non-lobbying project that serves the (c)(3)'s purposes, with records showing that use, doesn't count. The money must also stay out of any election work. Bolder Advocacy publishes a guide, with sample grant agreements, to granting unused lobbying room to a (c)(4) at year end.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) and its sister 501(c)(4) share an office and several staff. Name two practices that keep the (c)(3)'s money from paying for the (c)(4)'s lobbying or election work.
items.answer: Keep separate bank accounts and books; have shared staff keep time records; and split shared costs (salaries, rent, equipment) under a written cost-sharing agreement, with the (c)(4) reimbursing its full share on a regular schedule.
keys: separate bank accounts and books
time records for shared staff
a written cost-sharing agreement, with the (c)(4) paying its full share promptly
items.x: If deductible (c)(3) money pays for the (c)(4)'s lobbying or election work, the (c)(3) puts its exemption at risk. Alliance for Justice, which advises advocacy nonprofits, publishes a sample cost-sharing agreement and recordkeeping guides; it suggests reimbursing generally within 30 to 60 days, while noting there is no clear IRS guidance on timing.

choice.p: Which practice keeps a 501(c)(3) from subsidizing its sister 501(c)(4)'s political work when they share staff?
o: Staff log their time, and the (c)(4) repays its share of pay and rent under a written deal
The two groups share one bank account but label each payment with the group it belongs to
The (c)(3) pays all shared costs, and the (c)(4) makes a matching donation to it at year end
The (c)(4)'s board signs off on every expense the (c)(3) pays before the money goes out
ow: Mixing money in one account makes it hard to show the (c)(3) paid only for its own work.
A year-end gift that isn't tied to actual use doesn't show the (c)(4) paid its real share, and the (c)(3) fronts political costs all year.
Approval doesn't change who pays; the costs still need to be split by actual use.

items.p: Why is it legally simpler for a 501(c)(4) to give its sister (c)(3) free staff time or data than for the (c)(3) to do the same for the (c)(4)?
items.answer: A (c)(4) may do everything a (c)(3) does, so free help to the (c)(3) supports work the (c)(4) is allowed to fund. Free help from the (c)(3) could let deductible money pay for the (c)(4)'s lobbying or political work, so the (c)(4) must pay fair value for what it uses.
keys: the (c)(4) can do anything the (c)(3) can, so its help funds permitted work
free (c)(3) help could subsidize lobbying or politics with deductible money
so the (c)(4) must pay fair value
items.x: Alliance for Justice calls this the 'uphill / downhill' principle: resources move easily from a (c)(4) to a (c)(3), but moving them the other way takes payment at fair value and good records. The same logic is why a (c)(3) may not give a PAC anything of value for free.

choice.p: Why can a (c)(4) give its sister (c)(3) free help more easily than the reverse?
o: A (c)(4) may do charity work too, but free (c)(3) help could subsidize (c)(4) politics
A (c)(4) that controls its sister (c)(3) may treat both groups' assets as one pool
Gifts to a (c)(3) are deductible, so the (c)(4) earns a tax deduction for its help
A (c)(4) owes tax on help it receives, while a (c)(3) receives help tax-free
ow: Affiliates are separate legal entities with separate assets, even when one controls the other.
A (c)(4) is itself tax-exempt, so a deduction is worth little to it, and the rule turns on what the help pays for.
Both groups are tax-exempt and owe no tax on gifts they receive; the difference lies in what each may pay for.

items.p: A 501(c)(4) wants to use its sister (c)(3)'s 40,000-name supporter list to email people urging them to vote for candidates the (c)(4) has endorsed. What's the safest way to do it?
o: Rent it at fair market value, set by a list broker, and document the deal in writing
Use it for free, since the two groups share a mission, a board and supporters
Use it for free, as long as the (c)(4) pays the cost of sending the emails
Don't use it at all: a (c)(3)'s list may never be shared with a political group
ow: A shared mission and board don't change who owns the list; free use would let a deductible asset support partisan work.
Paying only the sending costs is below fair value, so the (c)(3) would still subsidize the (c)(4).
A (c)(3) may rent its list at fair market value; the risk lies in free or cheap use.
keys: rent at fair market value
valued independently, such as by a list broker, and documented
items.x: Alliance for Justice advises that a (c)(3) shouldn't give lists or data free to a (c)(4) for partisan use or to a 527, but should rent or sell them at fair market value, preferably through a list broker, and document each deal; for 527 renters it adds that the list should be equally available to other political groups. Adler & Colvin note that partisan use may call for extra precautions. Voter-registration data a (c)(3) collected carries extra risk and needs legal advice first.

items.p: A 501(c)(4)'s candidate endorsements sit on pages inside its sister (c)(3)'s website, under the (c)(3)'s banner and logo, with only the (c)(4)'s small logo added. What is the main legal risk?
o: The endorsements may be treated as the (c)(3)'s own, risking its exemption
The (c)(4) may lose its exemption for using another organization's trademark and logo
The endorsements will count against the (c)(3)'s annual limit on lobbying spending
None, as long as each group pays its own fair share of the website's costs
ow: No tax rule bars a (c)(4) from using an affiliate's logo, and a license can cover it; the exemption at risk belongs to the (c)(3).
Endorsing candidates is campaign intervention, which a (c)(3) may not do at all; the lobbying limit is a separate rule.
Splitting costs doesn't fix attribution if visitors can't tell which group is speaking.
keys: the endorsements could be attributed to the (c)(3)
putting its exemption at risk under the campaign-intervention ban
items.x: In a 2009 technical advice memorandum (binding only in that case), the IRS found a (c)(4)'s endorsement pages, housed on its (c)(3) affiliate's site under the (c)(3)'s banner, 'virtually indistinguishable' from the (c)(3)'s own pages and concluded the (c)(3) had intervened in a campaign. The (c)(4)'s payment of its share of site costs didn't change that. Practitioners recommend distinct names (such as an 'Action Fund'), separate branding, and labels saying which group endorses.

units.title: Funders and fundraising
units.desc: What private foundations, donor-advised funds and LLCs may fund, and the receipts, disclosures and 2026 tax changes that shape fundraising.

items.p: A private foundation wants to support a 501(c)(3) that lobbies on the foundation's issue. Which grant can it make without penalty?
o: A general support grant not earmarked for lobbying, even though the charity lobbies
A grant earmarked for lobbying, as long as the charity has made the 501(h) election first
Any grant at all, as long as the foundation lists it on its annual Form 990-PF
None: a private foundation may not fund any charity that does any lobbying at all
ow: The 501(h) election sets the charity's own limits; a grant earmarked for lobbying is still a taxable expenditure for the foundation.
Reporting a grant earmarked for lobbying doesn't cure it; the foundation still owes the tax.
Treasury rules expressly allow general support grants to charities that lobby.
keys: a general support grant not earmarked for lobbying
allowed even though the charity lobbies
items.x: Under Treasury rules, a general support grant isn't a taxable expenditure unless it's earmarked for lobbying. A project grant is also fine if it isn't earmarked and doesn't exceed the project's budgeted non-lobbying costs that year. 'Earmarked' includes oral agreements. A foundation that lobbies itself, or earmarks a grant for lobbying, owes excise taxes (with narrow exceptions, such as nonpartisan analysis).

items.p: Put in order the steps of 'expenditure responsibility' that a private foundation follows when it funds a 501(c)(4)'s charitable project.
items: Make a pre-grant inquiry into the (c)(4) and its plans
Sign an agreement limiting the money to the charitable project, with no lobbying or election use
Pay the grant, which the (c)(4) keeps in a separate fund
Collect the (c)(4)'s reports on how the money was spent
Report the grant and its use on the foundation's annual Form 990-PF
items.x: Grants to groups that aren't public charities, including (c)(4)s, LLCs and businesses, are taxable expenditures unless the foundation exercises expenditure responsibility and the purpose is charitable: a 20% tax on the foundation and 5% on managers who knowingly approve. The agreement must also require the grantee to repay misused funds and keep books. Grants to public charities need none of these steps. As of October 2026, Treasury's guidance plan listed these rules for possible simplification, but they were unchanged.

items.p: A private foundation's board member signed a binding pledge of $25,000 of her own money to her university. To spare her the expense, the foundation pays the pledge. The university is a public charity. Is there a problem?
o: Yes: paying a director's personal pledge is self-dealing, even though a charity gets the money
No: the money went to a public charity, so the payment serves a charitable purpose
No, as long as the director doesn't also claim her own tax deduction for the gift
Only if the pledge exceeds 5% of the foundation's assets, the self-dealing threshold
ow: Treasury rules say a payment that satisfies a disqualified person's legal obligation is ordinarily self-dealing, wherever the money goes.
Skipping the deduction doesn't cure it; the benefit is being relieved of her own debt. (A looser rule applies to donor-advised funds.)
Self-dealing has no size threshold; 5% is the foundation's annual payout benchmark.
keys: yes, it is self-dealing
the foundation paid a disqualified person's (a director's) legal obligation
items.x: Self-dealing rules bar most financial dealings between a private foundation and 'disqualified persons' (such as its managers, substantial contributors and their families), even at fair prices. The insider owes a 10% tax on the amount involved, rising to 200% if not corrected, and managers who knowingly approve owe 5%. Public charities face a looser test (excess benefit transactions, covered in the governance unit).

items.p: A private grantmaking foundation must pay out roughly 5% of its investment assets each year. Which spending counts toward that amount?
o: Grants to public charities, plus reasonable costs of its charitable grantmaking
A grant to another private foundation, which adds the money to its own endowment
A grant to a charity the founder controls, whatever the charity then does with it
Money the board moves into a general reserve for future grants, at its own discretion
ow: A grant to a private non-operating foundation counts only if the recipient pays it out by the end of its next tax year.
A grant to a group the foundation or its insiders control counts only if that group pays it out by the end of its next tax year.
Money set aside counts only for a specific major project, for up to 60 months, under strict conditions.
keys: grants for charitable purposes, such as to public charities
reasonable and necessary administrative costs of charitable work
items.x: The required amount is based on 5% of the foundation's investment assets, paid out by the end of the following year. A shortfall triggers a 30% tax on the undistributed amount, and 100% if it isn't fixed. The exceptions stop foundations from meeting the rule by parking money with related groups. Operating foundations, which run their own programs, are exempt from this tax.

lessons.title: Donor-advised funds, LLCs and donor privacy

items.p: Match each way of giving to its main tradeoff for a donor.
pairs: Private foundation
Deduction and lasting control by its founders, but a yearly payout rule and a public annual return
Donor-advised fund
Deduction now and grants later, but the sponsoring charity has legal control of the money
Philanthropic LLC
Can fund lobbying, politics and businesses, but no deduction until it gives to a charity
Gift to a 501(c)(4)
Can pay for unlimited lobbying, but isn't tax-deductible
items.x: A DAF is an account at a public charity (the sponsor); the donor keeps only 'advisory privileges' over grants. DAF grants to most groups other than public charities, such as (c)(4)s, need expenditure responsibility, and grants to individuals are taxable distributions. Gifts to a (c)(4) aren't deductible, though they are free of federal gift tax.

items.p: A donor asks her donor-advised fund to pay for two $500 tickets to a charity's gala, where she and her spouse will have dinner. What is the problem?
o: DAF grants that give the donor more than an incidental benefit are taxed, and tickets are one
None, because the gala benefits a 501(c)(3), which is exactly where DAF grants are meant to go
None, as long as she doesn't also deduct the value of the dinner on her own return
The charity owes the tax on the dinner's value, since it is the one that served the dinner
ow: Grants must also give the donor no personal benefit beyond an incidental one.
She took her deduction when she funded the DAF; the issue is the personal benefit, taxed at 125% of its value.
The tax falls on the donor who advised the grant (125% of the benefit) and on fund managers who knowingly agreed (10%); the charity owes none.
keys: DAF grants can't give the donor a more-than-incidental benefit
event tickets are such a benefit
items.x: Section 4967 taxes a donor 125% of a more-than-incidental benefit from a DAF grant, and fund managers who knowingly agree 10% (up to $10,000). In Notice 2017-73 the IRS said it views even a split, with the DAF paying only the deductible part of a ticket, as such a benefit; it also let a DAF pay a charity the donor pledged to if the sponsor doesn't mention the pledge and she claims no deduction. As of October 2026 no rules on these points had been proposed or finalized. The simple fix: buy the tickets personally.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) must show its annual Form 990 return to anyone who asks. What does the public copy reveal about its donors?
o: Gift amounts may appear, but donors' names and addresses are withheld
The names of everyone who gave $5,000 or more during the year
The names of everyone who gave more than $200, as for campaign committees
The names of its largest donors, listed with its officers in Part VII
ow: The charity reports its larger donors (generally $5,000 or more) to the IRS on Schedule B, but names and addresses are removed from public copies.
The $200 threshold applies to federal campaign committees and 527 political groups, not charities.
Part VII lists officers, directors and top-paid staff with their pay, which is public; it doesn't list donors.
keys: donor names and addresses are withheld from the public copy
larger donors (generally $5,000 or more) are reported to the IRS on Schedule B
items.x: Public charities list larger donors (generally $5,000 or more; many use a higher cutoff) on Schedule B for the IRS, but names and addresses stay off public copies. Private foundations and 527 political groups are exceptions: their donors are public. Since 2020, (c)(4)s don't report donor names to the IRS at all, though they must keep the records. In 2021 the Supreme Court struck down California's rule requiring charities to file their Schedule B donor lists with the state (Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta).

lessons.title: Receipts, disclosures and the 2026 tax changes

items.p: A donor gives a 501(c)(3) $1,000 in March and never gets a receipt. Her bank statement shows the payment. When she files her taxes the next April, can she deduct the gift?
o: No: at $250 or more she needs the charity's written acknowledgment, received by the time she files
Yes: a bank statement or canceled check is enough proof for a cash gift of any size
Yes, as long as the charity lists her gift on the Schedule B it files with the IRS
Yes: the charity owes a penalty for not sending a receipt, but her deduction stands
ow: Bank records suffice only for gifts under $250; at $250 or more the law requires the charity's written acknowledgment.
Schedule B is the charity's own filing; it doesn't replace the donor's acknowledgment.
The charity owes no penalty for a missing acknowledgment; the cost falls on the donor, who loses the deduction.
keys: no deduction without a written acknowledgment for a gift of $250 or more
received by the earlier of the filing date or the return's due date
items.x: The acknowledgment must give the charity's name, the cash amount (or a description of property), and whether the donor got anything in return, with a good-faith estimate of its value. 'Contemporaneous' means she has it by the earlier of the date she files or her return's due date, including extensions. The IRS notes charities typically send these by January 31.

items.p: A 501(c)(3) sells $250 tickets to its gala, where each guest gets a dinner worth $90. What must the charity tell ticket buyers?
o: In writing, that only $160 is deductible, with its estimate of the dinner's value
Nothing, since this disclosure is required only for payments of more than $250
That the full $250 is deductible, since the dinner is part of a charity fundraising event
That nothing is deductible, since each ticket buyer receives a dinner in return
ow: $250 is the threshold for the donor's acknowledgment; the quid pro quo disclosure applies to payments over $75.
Only the amount above the value of what the donor receives is deductible.
The part above the dinner's value is still a deductible gift.
keys: a written statement that only the amount above the benefit's value ($160) is deductible
a good-faith estimate of the dinner's value
items.x: A quid pro quo contribution is part gift, part purchase. For payments over $75, the charity must give a written statement, when it asks for or receives the money, saying the deduction is limited to the excess over the value of goods or services and estimating that value. The penalty is $10 per contribution, up to $5,000 per event or mailing. Token items and some low-cost membership benefits are exempt.

items.p: A 501(c)(4) with $2 million a year in revenue sends a fundraising email. What federal tax rule applies to the email?
o: It must say clearly that gifts aren't tax-deductible as charitable contributions
It must promise each donor of $250 or more a written acknowledgment, as charities do
It must be listed, with its recipients, on the group's Schedule B for the IRS
None: the tax rules on fundraising requests apply only to 501(c)(3) charities
ow: The $250 acknowledgment backs up a charitable deduction, which (c)(4) donors don't get.
Schedule B lists contributors, not solicitations, and since 2020 (c)(4)s don't report donor names on it at all.
Section 6113 covers non-charity exempt groups and political organizations, with a penalty of $1,000 a day, up to $10,000 a year.
keys: a conspicuous statement that contributions are not tax-deductible
items.x: Section 6113 covers (c)(4)s, unions, trade associations and 527 political groups whose gross receipts are normally over $100,000. The statement must be 'conspicuous and easily recognizable.' It's the mirror image of the charity rules: (c)(3)s document what donors may deduct, while other exempt groups must warn that donors may deduct nothing.

items.p: Match each change to charitable deductions in the July 2025 tax law, effective for 2026, to the taxpayers it affects.
pairs: People who take the standard deduction
May deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 joint) of cash gifts to public charities, though not gifts to DAFs
All itemizers
Only charitable gifts above 0.5% of adjusted gross income count
Itemizers in the top (37%) bracket
Each dollar deducted saves at most 35 cents in tax
Corporations
Only gifts above 1% of taxable income count, still capped at 10%
items.x: These changes come from Public Law 119-21 (the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act'), signed July 4, 2025, and apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 2025. The non-itemizer deduction also excludes gifts to supporting organizations. The law made permanent the limit allowing cash gifts to public charities of up to 60% of income.

units.title: When things go wrong
units.desc: How a group loses exemption and fights back, the limits on politically driven audits and leaks, and the criminal, state and donor-privacy risks beyond the IRS.

items.p: In 1975 the IRS ruled on an antiwar group whose main activity was protests where it urged demonstrators to block traffic and disrupt the work of government, breaking local law. Could the group qualify as a 501(c)(3) or a 501(c)(4)?
o: Neither: planning illegal acts is not a charitable or social-welfare purpose
Only as a (c)(4), since the bar on illegal purposes applies to charities alone
As both, because its goals of peace and disarmament were themselves charitable
As both, unless its members were later convicted of crimes at the protests
ow: The ruling denied both: illegal acts are not 'permissible means of promoting the social welfare' under (c)(4) either.
The ruling turned on the means: sponsoring planned law-breaking as the main activity showed an illegal purpose, whatever the goals.
No conviction was needed: the ruling rested on the group intentionally encouraging violations of local law.
keys: qualifies as neither a (c)(3) nor a (c)(4)
items.x: Rev. Rul. 75-384 said the 'intentional nature' of the encouragement ruled out treating it as an 'isolated or inadvertent violation'; lawful protest is fine. A related limit: in Bob Jones University v. United States (1983) the Supreme Court upheld revoking a university's exemption over racially discriminatory rules, holding a charity must not be 'contrary to established public policy.' In 2024 and 2026 letters, the House Ways and Means chairman cited Rev. Rul. 75-384 in asking the IRS to examine groups he said had supported unlawful protests, including campus encampments.

items.p: Match each way a group can lose its federal tax exemption to what sets it in motion.
pairs: Revocation after an audit
The IRS finds the group no longer qualifies; the group can protest, appeal and go to court
Automatic revocation
Three straight years without filing a required annual return or e-Postcard
Suspension under section 501(p)
A federal designation of the group as a terrorist organization
items.x: Only audit-based revocation comes with full appeal rights. Automatic revocation has no appeal, though the group can apply for reinstatement, sometimes retroactively. A 501(p) suspension lasts until the designation is lifted and can't be contested in any tax proceeding. In each case the IRS removes the tax benefits only; it has no power to shut the organization down, which can keep operating as a taxable entity.

items.p: Put in order the steps by which an IRS audit can end a group's exemption and the group can challenge that in court.
items: The IRS opens an examination and asks for documents
The IRS sends a letter proposing to revoke exemption
The group files a written protest, which goes to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals
The IRS issues a final letter revoking exemption
The group asks a court for a declaratory judgment under section 7428
items.x: The protest is due within 30 days of the proposed letter, and skipping it can lead a court to find the group didn't exhaust its IRS remedies. The court petition (Tax Court, Court of Federal Claims, or the federal district court in D.C.) is due within 90 days of the final letter. The group keeps its exemption until the final letter. The IRS may also tell state charity officials about a proposed revocation.

items.p: After an audit, the IRS mails a 501(c)(4) a final letter revoking its exemption. The group never filed a protest, and a month later it petitions the Tax Court under section 7428. What is its main legal problem?
o: It never protested to IRS Appeals, so it likely hasn't exhausted its remedies
Section 7428 covers only 501(c)(3) charities, so a (c)(4) has no route to court
It filed too late, since petitions are due within 30 days of the final letter
The Tax Court can't hear exemption cases; only a federal court of appeals can
ow: Section 7428 also covers other 501(c) groups, including (c)(4)s.
Thirty days is the deadline to protest the proposed letter; a court petition is due within 90 days of the final letter.
The Tax Court, the Court of Federal Claims and the federal district court in D.C. can all hear these cases.
keys: failure to exhaust administrative remedies
it didn't protest to IRS Appeals before going to court
items.x: A court can rule under section 7428 only if the group 'has exhausted administrative remedies available to it within the Internal Revenue Service,' and the IRS warns that a group that doesn't protest may be found not to have done so. The same section helps applicants the IRS ignores: remedies count as exhausted 270 days after a group applied, if it took all reasonable steps, so it can then ask a court to decide its status.

items.p: The IRS revokes a charity's 501(c)(3) status after an audit and announces it. Three months before the announcement, a donor who knew nothing of the problems gave $5,000. Can the donor deduct the gift, and on what basis?
o: Yes: unaware donors may rely on the IRS listing until the public announcement
No, because the revocation reaches back to when the charity stopped qualifying
Only the first $1,000, the most any individual may deduct once a charity loses status
Only if the charity later wins its court case and has its exemption restored
ow: A revocation can reach back for the charity itself, but IRS rules protect unaware donors until the public announcement.
The $1,000 cap is a separate rule for gifts made after the announcement while the charity's court challenge is pending.
Donor reliance turns on timing and knowledge: an unaware donor's gift made before the announcement stays deductible whatever a court decides.
keys: yes
unaware donors may rely on the IRS listing until a revocation is publicly announced
items.x: Under Rev. Proc. 2018-32, donors lose this protection if they knew of the revocation, knew it was imminent, or were partly responsible for the conduct behind it. The announcement can come in the Internal Revenue Bulletin or on the IRS website. Separately, section 7428(c) keeps gifts deductible, up to $1,000 per individual, from the announcement until a court rules, if the charity challenges in time; people responsible for the problems don't qualify.

items.p: Which route can take away a nonprofit's tax exemption because of a decision made outside the IRS, with no IRS audit and no challenge allowed in any proceeding about federal tax?
o: A federal terrorism designation, which suspends exemption under section 501(p)
A congressional committee's letter referring the group to the IRS for revocation
A written request from a White House official that the IRS revoke the group's status
A state attorney general's finding that the group misused its charitable assets
ow: A referral can prompt an audit, but revocation still runs through the IRS exam, appeal and court process.
Section 7217 makes it a crime for White House staff to request an audit of a particular taxpayer, and revocation still needs the IRS process.
A state attorney general enforces state law in state court; federal exemption remains an IRS decision.
keys: suspension under section 501(p)
triggered by a federal terrorism designation, with no IRS audit
items.x: Section 501(p), added in 2003, suspends exemption and bars deductions while a group is on a State Department terrorist list, is named in a terrorism sanctions order such as Executive Order 13224, or is named as supporting terrorism in an executive order that expressly cites 501(p). The group must attack the designation itself, and gets back overpaid tax if it proves erroneous. In 2003 the IRS applied it to three US charities, including the Holy Land Foundation. The September 2025 executive order calling Antifa a 'domestic terrorist organization' doesn't cite 501(p).

lessons.title: Pressure on the IRS and its limits

items.p: From 2010 to 2012, IRS staff reviewing exemption applications flagged groups with names like 'Tea Party' and 'Patriots' for extra scrutiny. In 2013 the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA) reported on it. What harm did TIGTA find?
o: Years-long delays and demands for unneeded information, such as donor lists
Most of the flagged groups were denied exemption in the end and had to shut down
Donors to flagged groups were audited using the lists the groups supplied
White House officials had written the screening criteria for the IRS staff
ow: None of the 296 cases TIGTA reviewed had been denied; 108 were approved, and 160 were still open after 206 to 1,138 days.
TIGTA reported needless requests for donor lists, and IRS officials said donor information they received was later destroyed.
IRS officials told TIGTA no one outside the IRS influenced the criteria; in 2015 the Justice Department closed its inquiry without charges.
keys: long processing delays, some over three years
unnecessary information requests, such as donor lists
items.x: TIGTA said the criteria picked groups by 'names or policy positions instead of indications of potential political campaign intervention.' A 2015 bipartisan Senate Finance Committee report, quoted in a 2017 TIGTA review, found most flagged groups were conservative but that the IRS also flagged some left-leaning applicants; TIGTA found criteria such as 'Progressive' and 'Occupy.' In 2017 the IRS apologized in a consent order settling a suit by 41 groups, and it later agreed to pay $3.5 million to settle a separate class action by 428 groups.

items.p: A written presidential directive tells the IRS Commissioner to make sure no tax-exempt groups finance political violence. Why might section 7217, which bars the President and senior officials from requesting audits, not clearly reach it?
items.answer: Section 7217 makes it a crime to request, directly or indirectly, that the IRS start or stop an audit or investigation of a particular taxpayer. A general directive about a category of conduct names no particular taxpayer, so it falls outside the ban's text.
keys: section 7217 covers requests about a particular taxpayer
a general enforcement directive names no particular taxpayer
items.x: Section 7217 (1998) covers the President, Vice President, their staffs and cabinet-level officials other than the Attorney General; IRS staff must report such requests to TIGTA, and violations carry up to 5 years in prison. Follow-up requests that single out named groups would raise a different question, since the ban covers requests made 'directly or indirectly.' The September 2025 presidential memorandum NSPM-7 contained a general directive of this kind. In September 2026 Senators Wyden and Warnock raised section 7217 concerns about reported Treasury reviews of named groups; as of mid-October 2026 those reviews were known publicly only through press reports.

choice.p: Why might section 7217 not reach a presidential directive telling the IRS to ensure no tax-exempt groups finance political violence?
o: It bans requests to audit a particular taxpayer, and this names none
It binds cabinet officers but exempts the President and Vice President
It covers criminal cases only, not the civil audits that lead to revocation
It applies only to oral requests, and this directive was put in writing
ow: The President and Vice President are the first officials the section lists.
It covers any request to 'conduct or terminate an audit or other investigation.'
It covers requests made 'directly or indirectly'; its few exceptions include forwarding a taxpayer's own written request.

items.p: Federal agents investigating a nonprofit for a non-tax crime want copies of the records the group itself gave the IRS during an audit. Under section 6103, what do they generally need?
o: An order from a federal judge, on reasonable cause that a specific crime occurred
Only a request, since an audit file stops being confidential once a crime is suspected
Nothing will work, because tax information stays inside the IRS in non-tax cases
Nothing beyond the group's Form 990, since the rest of the IRS file is off limits
ow: Audit files stay confidential; the law lists specific routes for sharing, each with conditions.
Section 6103(i) sets out several routes for sharing with law enforcement, including court orders and terrorism requests.
A 990 is public anyway under section 6104; other records can be shared through the routes in section 6103(i).
keys: an ex parte order from a federal judge or magistrate
reasonable cause to believe a specific crime was committed and the records are relevant
items.x: Records a taxpayer supplies generally need a judge's ex parte order under section 6103(i)(1). Information the IRS got from others is easier to share: an agency head's written request can be enough, the IRS may volunteer evidence of a federal crime, and terrorism investigations have their own request routes. Unauthorized disclosure is a felony (section 7213) and lets the taxpayer sue for damages (section 7431).

items.p: Match each way government power could be misused against a nonprofit to the legal protection that addresses it.
pairs: A White House aide asks the IRS to audit a named group
Section 7217: a crime, and IRS staff must report the request to the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration
An IRS employee leaks a group's donor list
Sections 7213 and 7431: a felony, plus damages the group can sue for
The IRS sits on an exemption application for a year
Section 7428: the group can go to court once 270 days have passed
A state regulator pressures a group's insurers to drop it
First Amendment: officials can't coerce private parties to punish speech
items.x: The NOM case shows the timing: an IRS clerk released its donor schedule (inadvertently, the government said), it was published in 2012, and the IRS paid NOM $50,000 in 2014. In NRA v. Vullo (2024) a unanimous Supreme Court let the NRA pursue its claim against a New York financial regulator who allegedly pressed insurers to drop it. Earlier episodes: the House Judiciary Committee's 1974 impeachment article charged President Nixon with seeking discriminatory tax audits, and the Senate's Church Committee found the IRS began a 1961 'test audit' of right-wing groups President Kennedy had criticized, later adding one left-wing group.

items.p: In 1956 Alabama demanded the NAACP's membership lists in a suit to bar it from the state. The NAACP refused and was fined $100,000 for contempt. What did the Supreme Court decide in 1958?
o: Forcing it to reveal its members would violate their freedom of association
The lists had to be produced, but sealed from public view
Alabama could demand them over the NAACP's failure to register in the state
Only members, not the NAACP, could raise the members' privacy rights
ow: The Court shielded the names from the state itself, given the risk of reprisals.
The Court found the members' names had no 'substantial bearing' on the registration dispute.
The Court let the NAACP assert its members' rights, since making members sue themselves would destroy the privacy at stake.
keys: compelled disclosure of members violated their freedom of association
items.x: The NAACP showed that identified members had faced 'economic reprisal, loss of employment, threat of physical coercion.' In Americans for Prosperity Foundation v. Bonta (2021) the Court applied the same idea to donors, striking down California's blanket demand for charities' donor lists: under 'exacting scrutiny,' disclosure rules must be narrowly tailored to the government's interest. The rule protects groups across the political spectrum.

items.p: A 501(c)(4) promises donors privacy, citing NAACP v. Alabama and AFP v. Bonta. Name two ways its donors could still be identified.
items.answer: Examples: a subpoena or document demand in a specific investigation (by prosecutors, a legislative committee or a state attorney general) that meets the constitutional test; an FEC report naming donors who gave over $200 to further the group's independent expenditures; a leak or mistaken release of records that contain donor names.
keys: a targeted subpoena or demand in a specific investigation
FEC reports naming donors who gave to fund independent expenditures
a leak or mistaken release of records
items.x: Bonta struck down an up-front demand covering every charity and pointed to narrower tools, such as a subpoena or audit letter in a particular investigation. Those demands still face 'exacting scrutiny': a substantial relation to a sufficiently important government interest, with narrow tailoring, which a targeted demand is better placed to meet. Leaks happen too: Bonta's challengers found nearly 2,000 confidential donor schedules posted on California's website.

choice.p: Which of these can still expose a (c)(4)'s donors despite NAACP v. Alabama and AFP v. Bonta?
o: An FEC report naming donors who gave over $200 to fund its independent ads
Its public Form 990, which names every donor who gave $5,000 or more
A public records request to the IRS for the donor list it keeps on file
The Form 8976 notice it filed at the start, which lists its founding donors
ow: Public copies of a 990 omit donor names, and since 2020 (c)(4)s no longer list donor names on the Schedule B they file.
Section 6103 keeps tax records confidential, and since 2020 (c)(4)s don't list donor names on their returns.
Form 8976 asks for basic facts such as the group's name, address, formation date and purpose; it asks nothing about donors.

items.p: A US human-rights group wants to train members of a group the State Department lists as a foreign terrorist organization to use international law to settle disputes peacefully. Under Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project (2010), is that legal?
o: No: it is banned 'training' or 'expert advice,' even with a peaceful aim
Yes: teaching peaceful methods is speech that the First Amendment fully protects
Yes, as long as no money, weapons or equipment ever reaches the designated group
No, and the human-rights group also can't publish op-eds backing the group's cause
ow: The Court upheld the ban as applied to this training, 6 to 3, reasoning that such help lends legitimacy and can be diverted to violence.
'Material support' covers services, training and expert advice as well as money; only medicine and religious materials are excluded.
The Court said the law doesn't reach independent advocacy, only support coordinated with or directed by the group.
keys: not legal: it is material support (training or expert advice)
banned even though the aim is peaceful
items.x: 18 U.S.C. 2339B bars knowingly giving material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization. No federal law creates a matching list of domestic groups (CRS; still true as of October 2026), though Florida and Indiana passed state designation laws in 2026. Support for domestic actors is a federal crime under section 2339A only if given knowing or intending it to be used for listed terrorism crimes. The foreign list changes: in 2025 the State Department added drug cartels and four European groups it called violent antifa groups. Check partners against the current list.

items.p: A European foundation gives a US nonprofit a grant for the nonprofit's own campaign on US climate policy. When would the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) require the nonprofit to register?
o: If it does US political work at the foundation's request, direction or control
Once foreign grants make up more than a quarter of the nonprofit's annual budget
Never, because FARA covers only people acting as agents of foreign governments
Only if it lobbies Congress directly, since campaigns aimed at the public are exempt
ow: Foreign money alone doesn't require registration; the test turns on whether the group acts at a foreign principal's request or direction.
A 'foreign principal' includes foreign organizations, companies and individuals as well as governments.
'Political activities' include trying to influence any section of the US public on US policy.
keys: acting at the order, request, direction or control of the foreign principal
while engaging in US political activities
items.x: In a 2024 advisory opinion the Justice Department said a US nonprofit funded by a foreign nonprofit needn't register because its work served its own goals and wasn't 'significantly influenced' by the funder. Exemptions can also apply, such as for groups registered under the Lobbying Disclosure Act when no foreign government or party is the main beneficiary. The International Center for Not-for-Profit Law advises against 'on behalf of' wording in grant documents. The September 2025 presidential memorandum NSPM-7 directed terrorism task forces to investigate nonprofits with close foreign ties engaged in FARA violations or money laundering that fund or support domestic terrorism.

items.p: Compared with the IRS, what power does a state attorney general typically have over a charity incorporated in the state?
o: Suing in state court to recover misused assets, remove directors or dissolve it
Revoking the charity's federal tax exemption after a state investigation finds misuse
Prosecuting its leaders for federal crimes such as material support for terrorism
Deciding whether the charity's application for federal tax exemption is approved
ow: Only the IRS revokes federal exemption, though it may tell state officials about proposed revocations.
The Justice Department prosecutes federal crimes; state attorneys general enforce state law.
The IRS decides exemption applications; states run their own charity registration.
keys: sue in state court to recover assets, remove directors or dissolve the charity
the IRS can end tax benefits but can't shut a group down
items.x: In New York the Trump Foundation agreed in 2018 to dissolve under court supervision, and in 2019 a court ordered Donald Trump to pay $2 million for misusing its funds. In the attorney general's suit against the NRA, a judge in 2022 refused dissolution, calling it 'the last option, not the first,' and a 2024 jury found executives liable. In 2025 the Texas Supreme Court let Texas's attorney general pursue a suit to revoke the charter of Annunciation House, a migrant shelter, without ruling on the merits.

units.title: Scenarios
units.desc: Founder and board situations that mix rules from the whole course: elections, lobbying, donors, affiliated groups, filings and investigations.

items.p: Your 501(c)(3)'s executive director wants to endorse a Senate candidate on her personal social media, where her bio lists her job title. Name two conditions that keep the post from counting as the charity's endorsement.
items.answer: She speaks only for herself; she uses no charity resources or official channels (the charity's accounts, newsletter, events, staff or money); and her title appears only for identification.
keys: she speaks in a personal capacity only
no charity accounts, publications, events or money are used
her title is used for identification only
items.x: IRS guidance (Rev. Rul. 2007-41) says leaders may speak 'for themselves, as individuals' but 'cannot make partisan comments in official organization publications or at official functions.' A leader's endorsement at a candidate's press conference was not the organization's; a personal column in the official newsletter was, even though the leader paid for the space. The same rule applies whatever the candidate's party. A sister (c)(4) or PAC can endorse instead.

choice.p: What keeps a 501(c)(3) executive director's endorsement on her personal social media from counting as the charity's?
o: She speaks only for herself and uses no charity accounts, money or events
Nothing, because any endorsement by a charity's top executive is the charity's own
She posts it after work hours, even if she uses the charity's own account
She runs it instead as a signed column in the charity's newsletter, paid for personally
ow: IRS guidance lets leaders endorse speaking for themselves, as individuals, with titles shown for identification.
The charity's own accounts are official channels, so partisan posts there are the charity's speech at any hour.
IRS guidance treats a personal column in an official publication as the charity's endorsement, even if the leader pays.

items.p: A challenger for a US Senate seat asks to speak at your 501(c)(3)'s annual gala. Her opponent hasn't asked. What does the IRS look at in deciding whether hosting her is campaign intervention?
o: Equal opportunity for her rivals at a comparable event, no endorsement, no fundraising
Whether she avoids naming her opponent, which alone makes a solo appearance acceptable
Whether she pays for her own seat, so the charity spends nothing on her appearance
Whether her opponent is offered a speaking slot at a smaller weekday meeting instead
ow: For a candidate invited as a candidate, the IRS asks whether rivals got an equal opportunity, whatever she says on stage.
The ban covers support even when it costs the charity nothing, so who pays for her seat doesn't settle it.
IRS guidance says a banquet for one candidate and a sparsely attended meeting for the other likely violates the ban.
keys: equal opportunity for other candidates for the same office, at a comparable event
no sign of support or opposition, and no campaign fundraising
items.x: Rev. Rul. 2007-41 lists these factors for candidates invited in their capacity as candidates.
