A candidate can also appear in a non-candidate capacity, such as an officeholder speaking on policy or an expert in her field, if the event doesn't mention the race and stays nonpartisan. A forum inviting every candidate, with neutral questions and moderator, is the safer format.

items.p: A donor offers your 501(c)(3) $50,000 'to fund lobbying for the clean-water bill.' What is the tax problem with accepting the gift on those terms?
items.answer: The donor can't deduct it: the IRS treats a gift earmarked for lobbying as nondeductible, even when it goes to a 501(c)(3).
keys: the donor's gift isn't deductible
because it is earmarked for lobbying
items.x: The position comes from Rev. Rul. 80-275 and a Treasury regulation barring deductions 'for lobbying purposes'; the nonprofit law site Nonprofit Issues notes the IRS will likely deny the deduction if it sees the earmark on audit. Fixes: the donor gives genuinely unrestricted support, leaving the charity to decide how much to spend on lobbying within its limits, or gives to an affiliated 501(c)(4), knowing that gift isn't deductible either. Either way, the charity's lobbying still counts against its own limit.

choice.p: A donor offers a 501(c)(3) $50,000 'to fund lobbying for the clean-water bill.' What is the tax problem?
o: The donor can't deduct a gift earmarked for lobbying
None, since gifts to any 501(c)(3) are deductible however a donor restricts them
The charity must list the donor by name on the public copy of its Form 990
The gift is deductible only if the charity has already made the 501(h) election
ow: The IRS has long held that gifts earmarked for lobbying aren't deductible (Rev. Rul. 80-275).
Public copies of a 990 omit donor names; donors appear only on the Schedule B the IRS keeps confidential.
The 501(h) election sets the charity's lobbying limit; it doesn't make earmarked gifts deductible.

items.p: Founders plan to have their 501(c)(4) run TV ads urging voters to defeat a Senate candidate, funded by three donors who each give $1 million for that purpose and want privacy. What should the founders tell the donors?
o: Because they gave to fund the ads, the (c)(4) must report their names to the FEC
A (c)(4) keeps donor names off its public filings, so their privacy is assured
They can deduct the gifts, since the (c)(4) is itself a tax-exempt organization
The ads are allowed only if the (c)(4) first registers with the FEC as a super PAC
ow: Public 990s omit donor names, but groups that make independent expenditures must report donors who gave over $200 to further them.
Gifts to (c)(4)s generally aren't deductible as charitable contributions.
A (c)(4) may make and report independent expenditures itself, as long as election work isn't its primary activity.
keys: donors who gave over $200 to fund the ads are reported to the FEC
items.x: Federal law requires anyone making independent expenditures over $250 to identify donors who gave over $200 'for the purpose of furthering' one; a 2018 court ruling struck down a narrower FEC rule, so donors whose gifts weren't for political purposes are generally not reported. The fix: tell donors up front that gifts made to fund the ads will be reported. A (c)(4) may do some election work but not as its primary activity, and its political spending can be taxed under section 527(f).

items.p: Your 501(c)(4) wants to use its sister 501(c)(3)'s email list for a fundraising drive. How should the (c)(3) let it?
o: Rent it at fair market value under a written agreement
Lend it free, since the groups share a mission and most of a board
Refuse, since a (c)(3) can't share assets with a group that lobbies
Lend it free if the (c)(4) promises not to use it for lobbying
ow: Free use means deductible (c)(3) assets subsidize the (c)(4), which can put the (c)(3)'s exemption at risk.
Practitioner guides list renting lists at fair market value to other organizations as a permitted (c)(3) activity.
Any free use is a subsidy, whatever the (c)(4) does with the list.
keys: rent at fair market value
under a written agreement
items.x: Alliance for Justice lists renting mailing lists 'at fair market value' as allowed for (c)(3)s, and law-firm guidance calls for a written contract for any (c)(3) resource a (c)(4) uses. Extra care is needed if the list will serve candidate work: the IRS treats renting a list to one candidate's campaign while turning others away as campaign intervention (Rev. Rul. 2007-41).

items.p: Your new treasurer finds that your small charity, which could have filed the short 990-N e-Postcard, filed nothing for three years. It now appears on the IRS automatic revocation list. What is the best fix?
o: Apply for reinstatement within 15 months under the streamlined retroactive process
Protest to IRS Appeals within 30 days, as a group would after a revocation from an audit
File the three missing e-Postcards, which restores the exemption automatically
Petition the Tax Court for a declaratory judgment restoring status under section 7428
ow: The IRS says the law gives no appeal from a proper automatic revocation; the route back is reinstatement.
Late filings don't undo the revocation; the group must apply again and pay the user fee.
Section 7428 reviews IRS determinations once a group has exhausted its IRS remedies; for automatic revocation the remedy is reinstatement.
keys: apply for reinstatement (for example on Form 1023-EZ) within 15 months
the streamlined process makes it retroactive to the revocation date
items.x: Revocation takes effect on the due date of the third missed return. A small group eligible for the 990-EZ or 990-N that hasn't been auto-revoked before can be reinstated back to that date if it applies within 15 months of the revocation letter or listing. Donors may deduct gifts made before the group's name was posted, if they didn't know. A reinstated group stays on the list, with its reinstatement date shown.

items.p: Your 501(c)(4) receives an IRS letter opening an examination of its political spending. The executive director wants to delete old internal emails before the agent's first visit. What should the board do first?
o: Bring in experienced counsel and suspend routine deletion of anything relevant
Let the deletion go ahead, since the group's retention policy already allows it
Set the letter aside, since an examination, like a compliance check, is voluntary
Have staff answer the agent directly, without lawyers, to show good faith
ow: Destroying records in contemplation of a federal investigation can be a crime under 18 U.S.C. 1519, and a written policy doesn't excuse it.
Only a compliance check, which the IRS labels as one, is voluntary; an examination can be enforced by summons.
Groups may have representatives, and an IRS interview must pause if the group asks to consult one.
keys: bring in experienced counsel
preserve records by suspending routine deletion (a litigation hold)
items.x: The IRS's own Form 990 instructions warn that the Sarbanes-Oxley ban on destroying records 'with the intent to obstruct a federal investigation' applies to exempt organizations. The International Center for Not-for-Profit Law also advises naming one point of contact for the IRS and the press. An examination can end with no change, with taxes, or with revocation, and the group keeps its exemption while it protests and appeals.

items.p: After reading about politically charged reviews of nonprofits, your board asks what to put in place now so the group is easier to defend if it is investigated. Name two practices.
items.answer: Examples: complete, accurate 990s and clean books; written document retention and whistleblower policies, with a way to suspend deletion; separate accounts, time records and cost-sharing agreements among the (c)(3), (c)(4) and PAC; counsel experienced in IRS and criminal matters identified in advance; D&O insurance that covers investigation costs; one designated contact for regulators and press.
keys: clean books and accurate filings
a written retention policy that can be suspended
documented separation among affiliated groups
counsel and investigation-covering insurance lined up in advance
items.x: These steps track guidance from the International Center for Not-for-Profit Law and the Nonprofit Resiliency Network, whose D&O guide warns that coverage of an investigation depends on how a policy defines a 'claim,' and that fines are usually excluded. Form 990 asks whether a group has written whistleblower and retention policies. Nonprofit lawyer Ellis Carter notes that the groups best placed are those whose compliance file 'was already in order before anyone was looking for a reason to open it.'

choice.p: Which of these makes a nonprofit easier to defend if it faces a politically charged investigation?
o: A written records policy that can be paused once an investigation looks likely
Keeping no written policies, so investigators have no policy to say the group broke
Running the (c)(3), (c)(4) and PAC from one bank account to keep the books simple
Telling donors their names can never be disclosed to any government body
ow: Written policies followed in practice help show good faith, and Form 990 asks whether a group has whistleblower and retention policies.
Mixing funds makes it hard to show that (c)(3) money didn't pay for political work.
Targeted subpoenas, FEC reports and leaks can all expose donors, so the promise can't be kept.
